Thousands of curious jammed the

VATICAN CITY, April 10 GIN.
SJ.-AssiSting the cardinal cele-
brant from his throne. Pope Plus
x1 today conducted the Good Fri
day pontifical mass in the Sistine
Chapel.


The ceremony, carried out in
the same manner as yesterdays
pontifical mass, was even more
impressive and solemn, containing
rituals performed only on Good
Friday.


Two cardinal deaconS and
Prince Marcantonio Colonna, he
reditary assistant of the threshold,
were in attendance at the papal
throne.


Pope Plus arrived in the great
chapel amid profound silence. He
wore red vestmentS. He did not
wear his episcopal ring nor did he
bless the faithful who were pres
ent.


Blessing Sunday


On this day Of the year no Cath.
olic bishop wears the ring of his
sacred office. And as the Bishop
Of Rome, the Pope also observes
this tradition. At the funeral
mass the blessing is reserved for
the dead, and therefore he alb
stained from blessing the living.
He will bless them on Sunday
from the exterior terrace Of the
Vatican baSilica.


At the termination of the gospel
the pontifical curSors closed the
great door and the apostolic
preacher delivered a sermon on
the Passion in Latin. He con-
Guided with the announcement the
Pope had granted an indulgence
Of 80 years to all present.


While the solemn ritual pro-
ceeded, the cardinal celebrant un-
covered the Holy Cross. He placed
it upon a purple cushion on the
steps of the altar for the Adora-
ton.


~ Kisses Cross


Several assistants of the cham
Der approached the throne and
took from the Pope his mantle
and his shoes. He descended
from the dais and took off his
mitre. genuflecting three times
and kissing the cross.


At this instant everyone in the
chapel prostrated himself and
did not rise until the Pontiff
had returned to the throne. Then
cardinals, prelateS, priests and
members of the papal court ap-
preached the Cross in their bare
feet for their act of alteration.


Beside the Cross had been
placed another cushion on which
rested a purse Of red velvet.
Into this the Pope deposited the
traditional contribution, followed
by cardinals and other church
dignitafies.


Veil AIKEN from CrucifiA
When the cardinals resumed
their seats the veil was removed
from the great altar crucifix and
the six candles lighted.


In silence the cortege then pro-
ceeded to the Pauline Chapel for
the Sacred Host. The Pontiff
walked beneath his canopy Of
state carrying the Sacred Host, sur
rounded by the cardinal deacons
and by his court Of MOBILES


When the Pontiff returned to
the Sistine Chapel, where mean
while the. relic of the Holy Cross
had been exposed, he placed the
Consecrated Host upon the altar.
This completed the Missa Pr ssanti-
ficatun.


The Holy Father then returned
to the vestment chamber where
he took off his vestments and
then withdrew to his apartment.

Bands of dog monsters-some of them
probably the biggest and fiercest beasts
of prey that ever lived-trooped over

ago.


One of these dogs, the dinocyon, was
as large as the Kadiak bear Of the
present day and probably looked much

Der of the canine family. 1t is known

Another, the meSocyon, was small, but
may have been more savage. The first
complete skeleton of this animal has just
been unearthed in Nebraska by paleon-

and study of the bones indicates some
possible relationship to the true canine
family, made up of the dogs, wolves, foxes
and hyenaS The actual order of ami

ever, has long since vanished from the
earth. Hitherto the family has been
known, for the most part. from scattered
bones from which it was necessary to
reconstruct an entire animal. In this
case only the right legs were missing.


These ancient dogs had very large,
formidable teeth. The probabilities are
that they were largely feeders on car
rion or that they stalked their prey
rather than actually chased it. From
the structure of their legs they appar-
emily were not good runners. Neither,
for that matter, were any of the ancient
animals upon which they fed.


Few archaeological questions are
more in dispute than that of the actual
ancestry of the true dog family, which
was spread all over the world at the
time when man first came on the scene.
1t now is generally supposed that this

Nebr.


This region was about the center of
the great camel distribution in North
America which lasted for more than
100000 years from the beginning of
the Eocene, or dawn age of mammals,
to the coming of the ice sheets. Titano-
tylopus probably represented one of the
closing stages of the development Of

originated in North America, emigrated

stock arose, and to the Old World, where
their descendants still survive.

Singapore ana Hongkong are

have much to offer, especially

Hongkong, with its famous hills,
its harbor with the peculiar blue
green of its waters, its pleasant
subtropical weather, except in sum-
mer, has much to offer the visitor.
Then, too it is a facinating mix
ture of the Orient and the Occi-
dent, with cricket field and solid
mercantile establishments con-
trasting with the native quarters.


Hongkong is a monument to
British law and order, in some
things typically British and per-
hapS rather Stolid and Stuffy, even
If it is the Orient. But this, too,
adds to the interest of the place.


Hongkong proper is a rocky
little island some II miles long
and from two to five miles wide.
off the Chinese mainland, near
the Pearl River and Canton.


Five miles across the bay. on the
mainland, is Kowloon, also British,
with it's big hotel and the towers
of the Kowloon-C Canton railway
station, landmarks visible for
miles.


Ferry boats shuttle to and fro
between Kowloon and Hongkong,
across the lovely harbor with its
liners and freighters from all over
the world, and its huge gray war
ships flying the British flag.


The warships, like the statue of
Queen Victoria, the cricket fields,
the seaside parks, all remind nos
talgic Britishers of home and make
it little easier to bear exile from
Pail Mall and the Strand.

MADRID, April IA series Of

cause a near-panic today during a
military parade in celebration of the
fifth anniversary of the founding Of
the Spanish Republic.


Several persons were trampled upon
as the crowd, terrified by the loud ex-
plosions, fed.


The explosions echoed through the
streets of the capital like machine gun
fire, but actually the effect was pro-
duced by series Of petards.


Diplomats Hear Blasts.


Police and assault guards rushed in
the scene and soon brought the crowd
under control.


The explosions occurred near the
box where diplomats and their guests
were viewing the parade, but none
was injured.


Among the spectators was Claude
G. Bowers, United States Ambassador
to Spain, who heard the explosions.


The threatened panic was placed
under control quickly, and the parade
continued without interruption.


Spain celebrated the fifth anniver-
sary with jubilant observances by Re-
publicans throughout the country.


Great Crowd Present.


A great crowd, despite drizzling rain,
watched a parade of artillery, infantry
and cavalry here while Premier Manuel
Azana and Acting President Diego
Martinez Barrio, holding Office until
successor to the deposed President
Niceto Alcala Zamora is elected, took
salutes. Republican flags few through
out the capital.


Heavy precautions were taken to
keep the day peaceful.

CLEVELAND, June 13.-Lady lob
byists, pretty triumphant about what
they got from the Republicans here,
turned their amazing energies today
toward Philadelphia and the Dem
ocrats.


For the first time, the business
woman, as such, had stuck her finger
into the political pie and pulled out
o plum.


It was the single sentence platform
plank saying: I'VE are opposed to leg
islation which discriminates against
women in Federal and State en-
ployment."


For the fifth national campaign
year, the League of Women Voters
had drummed on that. Others had
done so as far back as 1868 platform
writing. They got some encourage
ment this year from the platform
itself. more from the nominee, Gov.
Landon Of Kansas.


What Sentence Means.


Though the single sentence didn't
say so, the business women know, and
know that the candidate knows. it is
aimed straight at section 2l3 or mar
ried persons clause" of the economy
act, under which far more women
than men have been dropped from
Federal pay rolls due to having a
marital partner thereon.


Their drive was made through the
National Federation of Business and
Professional Women's Leagues. of
which politically astute Charl o. Will
liams is president. Able and alert
Jane Todd, New York Assembly,
woman, was steering. and had up-and-
coming Mildred Reeves, the late
Speaker Longworth's secretary, work.
ing on the Platform Committee.


The business women missed no bets.
In behalf Of their seemingly hopeless
plank, Mrs. Eugene Meyer, wife Of
the Washington publisher, got Gov.
Landon on the phone in Topeka, and
the tide changed overnight.


Telegram Is Hailed.


The League of Women Voters were
distinctly disappointed when the Re-
publican civil service plank didn't
specifically say something about post
masters. Their views were brought
to the attention of Gov. Landon. In
his electrifying telegram he said some
thing specifically about postmasters.
He said the merit system" should
apply to them all.


Both these groups use the technique
Of having leading Republican women
head their drive on the Republican
party; leading Democrats on the
Democrats.


Lena Madesen Phillips of New York
will head the business and professional
women at Philadelphia; Mrs. La Rue
Brown of Boston the League Of
Women Voters.

CHICAGO, Aug. 8-That eternal
triangle of the National League
has gone and laid the baseball
world by it's ears again.


Just when everyone thought the
circuits family affairs were all
Strengthened out with the Cubs as
head of the house for another year,
who should come romping back
but those TOUCHES from st. Louis
and say, "Sez YOU" While that
fight goes on there sit the Giants
waving big club and just waiting
for a chance to make it a three,
for-all.


The National League picture
stacks up like that today, just
seven weeks from the finish. Pick
your own winner; it's probably
wrong.


After dropping three out of four
to the Cards, it looked like the
Cubs had folded up their tent on
the leaders ground and were going
away from there. But smashing
14-to-5 victory in the finale yes
terday afternoon proved a power
full tonic. Not only the win, which
left them just two games in the
red, but the fact they found an
other use for their bats than as
hobby horses, inspired this from
Manager Charlie Grimm today:


"We're still in there and we're


in there to win. The team played


good ball throughout the series


despite the results and what's a


lot more important, think the


boys have snapped out of their


batting slump"


The Cubs undoubtedly have the
best pitching in the league and no
better proof of it can be found
than the way in which the staff
has held up during the past month
when they've had to pitch goose
eggs to win.


Frankie Frisch, on the other
hand, can simply point to the
standings. In fact, that seems
about the best thing the Cards
have to offer. They get there.


Naturally a few growls have not
made them league leaders. There's
Johnny Mize, who hits 'em where
they are, but over their heads;
Joe Medwick, Terry Moore, etc.
But nine good hitters can't make
a ball club-maybe the other fell
low has nine, too. A lack of
moundsmen to stop the other
guys may yet cheat the Cards out
of world series slice.


After all, Dizzy Dean does need
some time off to sleep. And who
else is there with brother Paul
gone? Jesse Haines is worthy
for the oldster he is; and then
there's Earnshaw. Parmelee,
Rhem, etc. But the latter three
usually all work on the same day
and have to be tabled as a unit.


The Giants are just waiting
their time to come in swinging.
That time will come in September
with corking fine windup to
the seasons schedule when they
play the second division on their
home grounds. The Cubs and
Cards, meanwhile, will be cutting
each others Threats with six
games right at the finish line.
The Giants, besides, have failed
to fall into their usual late sea-
son faint and are about the COM
INCEST team of the three. They
look like a good sleeper"

text:
Thunderstorms are meteorological
gypsies.


There are two big tribes of them wan
dering over the United States, following
rather definite routes from their GEN.
tiers year after year.


The thunderstorm distribution for 80
years has been analysed by William s.
Alexander of the staff of the United
States Weather Bureau, who finds some
striking Irregularities in their monthly re-
currence from year to year.


During the Winters, naturally, they are
in their southern quarters. The January
camp, scene of the greatest activity. Is
over Northern Louisiana. From this
center they are spread out thinly over
the Gulf and South Atlantic States as
far north as the Carolinas and over the
lower Missouri, Ohio and Tennessee val
leys, West of line drawn about through
the center of Texas they are practically
unknown. But, curiously enough. there
is a small thunderstorm center over
Northern Utah.


During February the Northern Louisi-
ana center shifts eastward. resting over
Mississippi. Southern Alabama and
extreme Western Florida. Also the
storms have started to spread over the
country The line has moved westward
to Southern Arizona and northward to
the Great Lakes, although still the
storms in these regions are very infre-
Quent.


In March the center shifts again. Dur
ING most of the month the greatest thun-
derstorm density, as shown by the 90
wear record, is found over Southern
Arkansas and extreme Northeastern
Louisiana. The area has continued TO
spread rather rapidly and now covers the
entire eastern half of the country. There
also has been a spread over Arizona,
New Mexico and Utah. During April
there is a slight westward shift OF the
center until it comes to rest over North
eastern Texas. Practically no part OF
the United States is entirely immune
from the storms during this month. AL
though they are quite rare along the
Pacific Coast, they are quite frequent in
the Southern Rocky Mountain States.


The May chart, says Mr.. Alexander,
reveals a very interesting and Slgnlfl-
cant development apparently not fore
Swallowed in any of the previous months
the sudden appearance OF secondary
center of activity on the West Florida
Coast in the vicinity of Tampa" This
marks the first appearance during the
year of the second gypsy tribe of storms.
All Winter they have been alternating
neutrality-suspicious. over the west
Indies. At the same time the first tribe
moves its camp northward into Missouri
and the Ohio and Tennessee valleys.


During June, 1t is shown by the 30-year
record, the storms have become common
all over the United States. The two
tribes" now are clearly distinct and
far apart. The Florida center has be-
come by far the largest and most active.
The Western, or secondary, center now is
established over Colorado. From each
center the storms spread out with de
minishing density. In the area of great
est activity the storms occur on an aver
age of every other day. About the west
ern center there is storm every three
days.


July. Mr.. Alexander finds, is the month
of greatest intensity over the entire
country. During this month the sec
ondary center over the Southwest has
about the same intensity as the primary
over the Southeast. The former has
had SIS days with thunderstorms in 80
years and the latter GAL. Curiously
enough, the Pacific Coast still is prac-
tically immune.

turned home Wednesday night.

Monday Tuesday and Thursday
nights. One came within a foot OF
hitting the couples infant son, they
said, and Michael Kelly, Mrs. Camp
bells uncle, was cut on the hand by
flying glass.

cidents, but had little to work on
Neighbors reported seeing an auto
mobile with West Virginia tags parked
near the home earlier in the week
with several men lettering near the
machine.

Bony structure cannot be
changed, but muscles can be
heightened and adipose tissue
thinned out. Today's exercises are
designed for stretching an d
smoothing the muscles of thick,
heavy legs.


Here Is an exercise which Is
marvelously effective:


Position: Put your right leg
forward, knee bent and weight
resting on bent knee. Thrust the
left leg back, knee straight. For
balance place the left hand on the
left hip.


Movement: Always keeping the
right heel on the floor, slowly and
forcibly increase the bend of the
right knee. Feel the pull on the
leg muscles? AS rapidly as pos
si5le increase the distance between
the two feet and intensity the
bending action at the knee, but
keep the heel on the floor. Repeat
with the bended left knee.


Do not overdo this exercise in
the beginning and then abandon
it. Take the movements slowly
and do the exercise daily and you
will be able to see an improve
ment in the lower leg contour.
This exercise takes persistence
but it brings results.


Here is another exercise for
stretching and lengthening leg
muscles.


Position: Roll back your shoul-
ders, weight braced with the ell
bows, legs extended back over
head with knees held straight.


Movement: Pulling toes to
ward the instep, point the heels
to increase the muscular stretch.
Now shuttle the legs rapidly for
fifty counts, keeping the knees
straight.


The most valuable part Of this
exercise is in curling the toes to-
ward the instep to increase the
stretch of the leg muscles.


You might as we'll get every
thing you can out of this exer-
else, however, and by keeping the
lower abdominal muscles drawn
up you can help maintain that
flat front line.

hurt, but practice it for perfect
legs:


Sit on the floor with the legs
stretched out in front, knees
straight. Now reach over and,
grasping the toes, pull them
toward the instep. Keep the
knees flat on the floor!

MIAMI, Fla, March 10 G.N.S.)
Five thugs early today robbed
the exclusive Hollywood Country
Club, swanky night resort 16
miles north of here, and escaped
with $4,000 in cash.


Harold E. Leopold, Chicago,
manager of the club, was struck
on the head with the butt of a
gun by one of the robbers when
he refused to open the safe.


Before entering the raiders
seized a guard stationed outside,
took his gun and forced him to
lead the way to the office where
Leopold and four employees were
counting the cash of the nights
business.


The men scooped up the cash,
tied Leopold, the guard and four
employees and fled.


The robbery was not discov-
cred until shortly after 10 o'clock
when other employees of the club
reported to work and found the
men bound.

NEW YORK, May 30.-Scraping
along at the years low, commodity
prices this week continued to reflect
the vagaries OF weather rather than
any pronounced slowing of demand.


The Associated Press weighted in
dex of 35 important wholesale COM
modify prices stood at 71.36, compared
with 7l.7s last week and 1918 a year
ago.


Better r-than-average rains occurred
in many of the States that were sub
normal on moisture, assuming the
proportions Of cloudbursts in some
parts of the Southwest. The great
plains, from Nebraska southwark, were
the chief beneflciaries.


The much needed moisture had
varying effects on the movements OF
agricultural prices. Cotton was higher
on reports that rains in Texas-largest
producer-were heavy enough to dam
age the stand in some areas. Oats
were steady during most Of the week,
closing fractionally higher.


Wheat Says Sharply.


Wheat tumbled sharply with the
rainfall in the No. Winter wheat
State-Kansas-which has felt mois-
ture deficiency all Spring. Although
the improvement was notable, Kansas
is still some 20 per cent below normal.


The largest Spring wheat States
North and South Dakota-are still
badly in need of rain. Spring wheat,
however, accounts for but 20 per cent
Of the total wheat outturn.


Corn and rye were lower, primarily
on the strength Of better moisture
news.


Live stock prices moved into low
ground for the year again, cattle and
lambs continuing weak. The decline
has been persistent during the past
several months-the index currently
being 90 per cent under its January
high. Hog quotations advanced against
the trend for the second week.


Food prices continued to move up
ward from the low established two
weeks ago. Cocoa has risen sharply
on what is understood to be tight
spot position. Flour forged ahead
despite the decline in wheat. Coffee
and butter lifted slightly. Lard gave
ground on the premise that a large
hog turnout can be expected this
Summer.


Keeps Narrow Range.


Industrial staples swung in mar
row range Just above the years low.
An advance in lumber was offset by
declines in rubber. turpentine, lin
seed oil and burlap.


Among the textiles: Cotton cloth
rebounded from the low levels Of the
previous week as low retail stocks
brought some good buying into the
market: wool and silk were both weak.


Tin dropped under the pressure Of
some uneasiness regarding the pro-
ducers' agreement.

NEW YORK. May 16.-Life-giving
rains spattering over dusty soil in
large sections of the Middle West
last week were largely responsible for
a further slump in commodity prices.


The Associated Press weighted index
Of IS important staples closed at
7l.65-just 04 above Thursdays low
for the year-aga:nst 72.44 last week
and 75.46 in the comparable period a
year ago.


Although rainfall for the country
as a whole has been slightly above
normal for the year through May IL.
according to Department of Agricul-
ture records, it has been a case of
large excesses in one section-the
East and Southeast-and deficiencies
in another-the Mississippi and Ohio
valleys.


More Rains Needed.


Recent rains, although alleviating
the parched condition of the Middle
West at least temporarily. still leave
many States far below normal as

Arkansas, 81 per cent below normal,
Oklahoma 48 per cent, Missouri 43,
Texas SO, North Dakota 80, Illinois
u, Kansas "a and Ohio %.

that such widespread moisture def
ciencies in late Spring could turn to
a serious drought condition unless
normal-or better rains are experienced
during the next two months.

Industrial commodities again

MADRID. Sept. 2 GN.S0.-The
road of anti-aircraft guns woke
Madrid from fitful slumber early
today when two insurgent air.
planes flew over the city.


The attempted air raid proved
abortive as the insurgent invaders
were put to flight before they were
able to drop any bombs. Gov
eminent pursuit planes and anti
aircraft guns cooperated in meet
ing this latest air threat to Madrid.


Alarm Sounds at Dawn


The air raid alarm was sounded
at daybreak. Militianfen were sent
racing through the city on motor
cycles, their sirens Screeching to
warn the population Of an i'm
pending attack. For the third time
in less than a week, there was a
scramble for Easements and other
safety points as searchlights at
tempted to pick out the raiders
and antiaircraft gunners swept the
skies for prey.


Madrid's defenders succeeded in
spotting the two insurgent planes
before any bombs could be dropped
and, Immediately, pursuit planes
streaked off on their trail.


The roar Of airplane motors,
defamation of anti-aircraft guns
and the screech of warning sirens
turned the city into bedlam. The
racket was clearly heard through
out the city and was doubtless
transmitted over telephone lines to
foreign capitals, leading to reports
the city again had actually been
bombed.


A thorough check-up, however,
indicated success for the loyalists,
with the only casualty motor
cyclist who lost control of his ma
chine while racing through the
streets and was severely injured.


More Americans to Leave


Meanwhile, the United States
Embassy renewed its urgent ap-
peal to all Americans to leave
Madrid Immediately. Fourteen
Americans, including 10 women,
announced their intention of leav-
ing for Alicante tonight to board
the cruiser Quincy. Embassy re-
ports state only about 70 Ameri-
cans remain in the capital.


An official war ministry COM
1nunique made no mention of the
heavy fighting which continues at
Trun. 1t stated:


There is little change on the
Estramadura front. Fighting at
Huesca continues fiercely, with
lOyalists striving to enter the
city before nightfall.


Fighting continues around
Cordoba. Oviedo and other
fronts are comparatively quiet"
In Madrid 100000 radical militia
men, government troops, women
and children staged a parade in
defiance Of what they called yes
terday's "abortive" insurgent air
raid.

clothing stores throughout the coun-
try last year was the best in seven
years for which figures are available,

expectations of the trade. Nation
wide survey disclosed today.

National Association of Retail Clo-
thiers and Furnishers pointed out
that the net profit for reporting stores
with a volume under 100000 was
442 per cent of gross sales compared
with 3.6 per cent. while the net for
larger stores was STA, against So the
previous year.

improvement, probably even in the
case of larger stores, since the vol
ume of sales increased. although this
was not measured by the survey. How
ever, the association said the result

profit that might have been expected.

per cent of gross sales. the highest

When Perry decided to cast his

the field wide open, but, judging
by past performances, Donald
Bulge, the wiry Californian, may
succeed to the throne vacated by
the black-haired Englishman.

mantown.

British title at Wimbledon but by

Forest Hills.

ford and Quist defeaEed Bulge and

the game meant nothing.

finals for the American title was
one Of the greatest matches ever
played anywhere. Bulge took the
first set, 60, dropped the next
two, 2-6, 6-S, captured the
fourth, 6-1, and lost the last,
80. The slim American was at
match point more than once, but
couldn't make the grade.

surprising upSets Of the year by
downing the defending champion,
Helen Wills, As, 6-3, 6-G.

of Stanford,d won the doubles
championship.

ever before in this country and
the crowds for the most part were
larger, but tournament tennis was
decidedly spotty in caliber.

Jimmy" Thomas, his eyes brimming
and his voice almost a whisper, pro-
nounced his own political obituary
today to hushed House Of Commons.


The veteran cabinet minister. who
was forced to resign as colonial sec
retary in the British budget scandal,
announced he would resign his par
liamentary seat at once and that he
would not try to come back.


He said it was my darkest hour"


Sir Alfred Butt, wealthy racing
enthusiast, who, judicial tribunal
decided, obtained official secrets from
Thomas and used them for private
gain, also gave notice he was quitting
his Commons seat.


Both denied again they had given
away or received any secrets. And
then both men, following ancient
usage, bowed to the speaker and left
the chamber.


Thomas, who once was an engine
wiper, said he had been urged to
recontest his House seat from Derby,
but that he had refused.

Two-year-old Charles Gum. jr.

home at 4437 Lowell street today

bulldog which might have cost him
his life.

the Corinthian Boat Club with his
mother when the dog, which weighs
about 60 pounds. playfully jumped
toward him and pushed him in the
water.


His father was some distance away
in his boat and Mrs. Gum could not
swim. Albert Seeley, steward at the
club, heard her frantic cries, however,
and jumped into the water and res
cued the child.


The boy was frightened by his sud-
den plunge. but swallowed little water
and recovered quickly. His father is
a naval research physicist.

Schacht, Reichsbank president and

Schacht, the Austrians, and Franz

cellor Schuschnigg number of times

Ernst Rudiger Won Starhemberg as

ported Italy had warned France that

many.

derstanding, but also Austria, Hun
gary and Poland-the first two

tria might consider an understand
ing with Germany provided the free

LURAY. Va. September l9-Carl

in the mountains. and when he finds

The practice of cooking veal in
sour cream, it is said, originated IN
Germany, as did sauerkraut and
many of our other sour and spicy
dishes.


Here is a recipe for that favorite
veal dish, wiener schnitzel, which
depends on sour cream, tomatoes
and paprika for its seasoning:


Wiener Schnitzel
2 pounds veal steaks
4 slices bacon, cut fine
2 tablespoons chopped onion
/ cup sour cream


1a cup tomato ketchup
l teaspoon paprika


Salt and pepper


Cut the veal steaks into indi-
vidual servings. Fry the finely
diced bacon. Dredge the slices of
veal in flour and brown, together
with finely chopped onion, in the
bacon fat. Season with paprika,
salt and pepper. Stir in the sour
cream and ketchup, cover, and let
cook slowly until the veal is done,
about thirty minutes.

By the Associated Press.


PITTSBURGH, October 27.-Secre-
tary of Labor Frances Perkins out
lined a program for proper economic
and social balance" at q community
forum last night.


In an address prepared for deliv-
cry, Miss Perkins said balance can be
obtained through the principles of a
national living wage, continuity Of
income, stability of employment. rea-
sonable profit and guidance for the
conservation and maximum utilization
of natural resources. She continued:


Fair and continued profits are Of
vital importance in industry. but good
and steady wages for workers and fair
prices for the produce of farmers are
also necessary to sound prosper
ity."


Secretary Perkins set forth the prog
ress she said had been made in labor
legislation and discussed activities OF
the United States Department of Labor
in the last three years. She said:


There has been more labor legisla-
ton in the States in the past three
years than at any other similar period
in the history of the United States.
Seven States have enacted minimum
wage laws since 1888; four have set up
labor departments and enacted factory
legislation, and three others have en-
acted workmen,s compensation laws.


Strikes have been few and amen
able to settlement in the last three
years. This has been SO because the
Government has not used the arm OF
force, direction and regimentation, but
instead has used the ancient art OF
conciliation and mediation. Strikes
have been settled, not beaten"

stand in the civil war

rebellion

by some strikers with their fight for
higher wages and other labor conces-

More than 5000 workers, arms

labor unions meetings planes for
Spain"

the 1000, ,000- worker total that greeted
Leon Blum when his Socialist govern
ment came into power was the cause
for worry and conjecture in many cir

Baby blue jays are among the most
charming Of bird juveniles.


Those particularly plaintive cries
which arise over the suburban areas at
this time Of year are from the little jays.
Most young birds are as large as, or
even larger than, their parents, but the
small blue jays are not quite as big as
theirs.


They have squat, durnpy appearance,
with ruffled feathers and voice which
fits into their generally helpless appear
ance.


All of the bold defiance of the adults Is
lacking in the little ones, who squeal and
squeak all day long for food, food, food.
The jaunty jays are fine parents.


All day long they heed the cries of
their little ones. making endless trips to
the place where the young birds are
flying about.


This place may be the nest, but more
often 1t is yard near the nesting place.
For all the young Of the bird popula-
ton are in the air now.


The baby wrens are out, the young
robins and mocking birds, the baby
wood thrushes and thrashers, the latter
sometimes hard to tell apart at a little
distance.


The longer legs, longer tail and bill
will help distinguish the thrasher young
from those of the thrush.


The wood thrush, as might have been
expected, is an exemplary parent. The
young stay close at hand in the garden,
with bills held open at all times for
dainty tidbitS which may be placed in
them.


These are the days, however, when all
young birds are learning how to hunt
food for themselves.


1t is interesting to see their first
tentative steps in this direction.


Young mockingbirds are adopts strik-
ing out early for themselves.


An amusing instance came to light
recently in a nearby Maryland garden.
Those who lived in the house attached
to the garden had never seen young
mockingbirds.


Tolerably familiar with the adult birds,
they totally failed to grasp that the
large, handsome fellows which were
walking around by the big tree were the
mockingbird babies.


What bird is that?"


The old cry of bird watchers went up.
The birds had white on them, but
were so round and shipshape under
meath very fat that no one recognized
them for what they were.


An eager search went on in the bird
books.


Could these be loggerhead shrikes?


Well, not exactly.


Some one with more common sense
than usual at last hit on the truth.


Why, they are baby mockingbirds!
Sure enough, they were.


This is one of the pleasures of bird

Just how they differ from the adults.

take their places almost instantly beside

ing and fastened themselves to the

The mother duck lays her eggs by

SEATTLE, June 13.--The Alaska
season stepped to the front this week
with the initial sailings and advance
bookings voicing healthy indications
that season supreme was on the
threshold for the Northern wonder
lands. Prominent in the passenger
lists were the wide representations
from nearly every State in the Union,
according to tourists and steamship
officials, who foresee a season of rec
ord travel, drawn from both East and
West. Many tours are featuring Lake
Atlin and the White Pass districts.


Lake Atlin, which stretches over 80
miles, is a vision of grandeur, eXcelled
in few parts of the world. The secluded
garden lands visited are topped by
snow-white peaks above immense
tracts of forest greenery and robed In
bright flowers.


The White Pass voyage is through
Lake Laberge, White Horse Rapids and
the famous Thirty Mile River. Passing
Five Finger Rapids the 175-mile
steamer journey to Dawson eliminates
into scenic waterway passage, framed
by giant rising palisades, which edge
and recede into picturesque vistaS.
Dawson, once the mining camp objec-
tive of the long trail, now is an ultra
modern city, with charming homes,
gardens, parks, fine hotels. Motor
roads lead to many famous totem vii
lagos.


Four itineraries include visits to
Ketchikan, Wrangell and the Taku
Glacier voyage. At Juneau a sight
seeing journey may be made of the
gold mines, with motor tour to AUX
Lake and Mendenhal Glacier. Skag-
way, once known as the boom town in
gold rush days, will entertain visitors
by its famous Blanchard gardens,
considered one of the finest in the
world. The vast garden patches will
serve to introduce the riotous bloom
of Alaska lands in Summer flowers.
Sitka, the once romantic Russian
town and beautiful capital city, adds
novelty by its "lovers' lane" through
totem pole lined villages. Itineraries
include Mount Mckinley National
Park after stops at Cordova, Valdez,
the journey through the Columbia
Glacier, Fairbanb ind Seward.

Head and shoulders above other

COSHHOCTON, Ohio, April 25.-
Quiet prevailed here today with both
police and interested parties unwilling
to predict future events in the month
old strike of the indianapolis Glove
Co. plant.


A night during which fists were
swung freely, clothes torn, tear gas
guns held ready. and rotten eggs and
vegetables hurled at house affording
haven to 20 besieged non-union woman
workers. ended only when police per-
suaded a yelling crowd OF 500 to dis
perse.


The crowd besieged the 20 women in
the home of Hannah Turner, one of
their number, for several hours, throw
ing old eggs and soft vegetables freely.
The women had taken refuge there
when quarrels broke out during a
truce.


Fifty non-striking workers, mostly
women, worked in the plant all day
yesterday. Strikers and sympathizers.
disregarding a non-interference in
junction, besieged them and spiked
the plant doors shut.


A crowd milled about the plant at
quitting time and refused to let the
workers leave. A union organizer,
James Taylor, broke the impasse by
agreeing to let the workers leave if
they would promise not to re-enter the
plant until contempt citations against
pickets were settled.

Mrs. Amy L. Veerhoff, 604 Aspen
street, long prominent in social service
and educational work here, died yester-
day after a long illness in Emergency
Hospital.


Mrs. Veerhoff, wife of Otto L. Veer-
hoff, formerly was chairman Of the
board of the National Training School
for Girls, having been appointed by
President Harding and reappointed BY
President Coolidge.


At various times, Mrs. Veerhoff was
president of many organizations, in
Guiding the local branch of the Amer
ican Association of University Women
the College Women's Club, the Takoma
Park Women's Club, the Takoma Park
Home and School Association, the
Takoma Park Friendship Club, the
Takoma Park Baptist Ladies' Aid Asso-
citation and the Columbia Junior High
School Parent-Teacher Association.
Farm and Garden Head.

president of the National Capital
Division of the Women's National
Farm and Garden Association. She
was member of the Twentieth Gen.
tury Club, the Juvenile Protective
Association. the District Federation Of
Women's Clubs and the Social Hygiene
Society. Likewise, she was active in
the Young Women,s Christian Associa-
tion, the Monday Evening Club the
Florence Crittenton Association, the
English Speaking Union and the Vassar
Alumni Association.


A native of Fort Scott, Kans., Mrs.
Veerhoff was educated at Lake Erie
College, Vassar College and George
Washington University, graduating

proprietor of the veerhof Art Gallery

1850 Pennsylvania avenue. The body

MADRID, November l8.-Packed
four-deep in subway stations. terrified
men, women and children made an
underground city of bombarded and
besieged Madrid today.


Quarreling and jostling for elbow
room or even curling up on the plat
forms beneath the shuff1ing feet of
the crowds, Madrilenos sought safe
refuge from aerial bombs and artil-
lery shells while Fascist invaders and
defending militiamen fought house to
house in a corner of the city.


Tanks Reported in City.


(Unconfirmed advices from In
surgent sources just outside Madrid
said Fascist tanks and armored cars
were standing on the Paseo De
Rosales in Madrid, after crossing into
the city over a military bridge)


Many of those who jammed the
subway stations tried to push aboard
trains running to the eastern sections
of Madrid and away from the bonn
barded western and central portions


The exodus to the eastern area be-
gan after Fascist bombers rained ex-
ploslves and insurgent gunners sent
a barrage Of shells ripping into the
business and residential districts.


Few Madrilenos slept during the
night as the thunder of a terrific
bombardment from Fascist batteries
echoed throughout the terrorized city.


Fires Rage.


Fires blazed in the central district
as insurgent invaders threw all avail
able man and gun power into the
drive to capture Madrid.


The northwestern section was trans
formed into virtual no-man's land

building-to-building battles in the
University City district.


The flood of refugees crowded to

Lines of men and women four deep
formed before the train doors. Fami-
lies quarreled with one another for

Mothers warmed milk for their

refugees sat on the bare platform
floor eating their dinner. which they
had brought with them. War-weary
soldiers arriving on trains from the
government barricades fell out of the

ANNAPOLIS, Md, May 30.-A gal
liant episode in the sea annals of the
Nation-the burning of the frigate
Philadelphia in the harbor of Tripoli
was re-enacted tonight as the Naval
ACADEMY launched its annual June
week festivities with color and pag-
eantry.


President Roosevelt watched the re-
enactment from the deck of the Po-
tomac, moored off the academy. The
President boarded the yacht earlier in
the day and took turn out in Chesa-
peake Bay.


Fifteen thousand spectators saw
how young Stephen Decatur, on Feb
ruary Is, 1904. entered the harbor
OF Tripoli, overcame the Corsair crew
Of the captured frigate and burned
and sank it at its anchorage.


Escape Under Gunfire.


The crowd saw the youthful cap
tain and his crew of 81 men and 4
officers escape from the harbor amid
the thunder of guns from the Tripo-
Titan forts and pursuing vessels.


The reproduction of the historical
episode was followed by visit Of
King Neptune, who boarded the de-
stroyer Babbitt and exchanged greet
jngs with Rear Admiral David Foote
Sellers, superintendent of the acad-
emy. Neptune, with mermaids (all
midshipmen) reviewed a parade of
illuminated sub-chasers, patrol boats
and ketches.


The city Of Tripoli was repro
duced on the tennis courts. The three
upper classes of midshipmen with
their parents and friends ate supper
in the streets of the canvas city while
costumed Corsairs strolled about, some
playing musical instruments.


The original Philadelphia, block
aiding Tripoli during the war with the
Barbary Corsairs, ran aground and
was captured by Corsairs. Commodore
Preble, commanding the American
squadron, determined to destroy the
frigate and selected Decatur for the
task.


When the supper, which represented
the joy of the Tripolitans at the cap
ture, was finished, all the lights about
the basin were extinguished.


Americans Discovered.


From the darkness the Intrepid
manned by Decatur" and his crew,
crept into the harbor. As it did 1873
years ago, the small boat ran along
side the Philadelphia and sought per-
mission to tie up to her hawser This
was granted but. as the bow of the
Intrepid got under the anchor chain,
a cry of "the Americans" arose.


The spectators watched the battle
for the frigate and its recapture. Sud-
denly they saw red fire shoot up from
the vessel and spread through its rig
ging. Decatur" and his crew began
pulling rapidly away, from the sinking
ship.


A thunder of cannon fire broke out
as two imitation forts opened up and
Tripolitan gunboats took up the pur-
suit. Red, white and green flares, sent
up from the forts gave a weird touch
to the scene


Relatives and sweethearts of grad
uating midshipmen, naval officers and
sports lovers made up the holiday
crowd which thronged to Annapolis
J hours before the sports events against
Army formally opened the week. June
week ends Thursday when approxi-
mately 263 midshipmen receive di-
plomas.

ticipate in the treaty because of ex-
isting sanctions for her aggression in
East Africa.

HERRYvIILE, Va. July 18.-De-
spite the efforts of friends and neigh
bors to clear her. Mrs. May Small
wood, As, was named here late yes
terday as the slayer of three members
of her family before taking her own
Life.


Finding that Mrs. Smallwood had
gone temporarily insane early last
Monday. Magistrate Luther Thomp-
son issued a certificate stating that
she killed her two sons and her
mother with a shotgun. then turned
the weapon on herself.


The other victims were Mrs. Susan
Virginia Elsea, S7-year-old Blue Ridge
Mountain Sunday school teacher, and
Ebert and Akin Smallwood, % and
II years old, respectively.


Version Of Tragedy.


The story of the tragedy. as un-
folded during the coroner's inquest
yesterday, was, IN brief, as follows:


Mrs. Smallwood, In poor health ana
fearing an operation. awoke Monday
morning just after daybreak. Dress
ing quietly IN the first-f1oor bedroom
of their log cabin home tucked away
In the Blue Ridge Mountains nine
miles east of here, she took shotgun
and climbed to the attic, where her
two sons were sleeping.


First, she shot Ebert through the
back of the head as he slept. The
noise aroused Akin, but the deranged
mother reloaded hastily and fired a:
him. The boy probably was killed in
stantly, but fearing he might survive,
Mrs. Smallwood stood over him and
fred another charge into his body
from the single -parreled weapon.


Then she went back downstairs,
where her terrified mother, a helpless
invalid, lay In bed Reloading again,
she shot Mrs. Elsea through the left
lung.


The beds Of the three victims were
then saturated with kerosene and set
afire


Calmly removing her shoes, Mrs
smallwood then ignited her own bed
laid down on it, placed the shotgun
nnuzzle under her left arm and fired.


When neighbors, attracted by the
smoke, broke into the house, all four
beds were burning. They also found
the charred remnants of pocketboos
and two Of the discharged shells on
q burning wash stand.


Say Health Improved.


Several neighbors testified that Mrs
smallwood's health had been improv-
ing and denied she was contemplating
an operation. They insisted there was
nothing about her conduct to indicate
she was mentally deranged.


Sergt. Francis Funk, Winchester
ballistics expert. testified, however
that the only hngerprints found On
the gun and lamp presumably used
in saturating the beds were those OF
Mrs. Smallwood.


Two witnesses said Mrs. Elsea was
tied In her bed when they reached the
scene, a peculiar circumstance that
was not cleared up. Her son, Joseph
Elsea, testified, however, that she
broke her hip several years ago and
used a rope tied to the footboard tc
pull herself around in bed. 1t was
suggested this rope may have become
wrapped around her body in some
way, giving her the appearance OF
being tied.


: When police reached the scene, the
shotgun was found on the dining room
table, but one of the neighbors testi-
fed he found it on Mrs. Smallwood' S
bed and placed it on the table when he
FIRST reached the cabin.

The Democrats reply to Governor

Roosevelt administration ira d e

today by Secretary of State Cor
dell Hull.


Hull dubbed untrue Republican
charges that the treaties have done
more harm than good. He de.
clared the reciprocal trade treaties
have proved the most vital factor
in returning prosperity. Several
times he specifically used the Re
publican presidential nominees
name in referring to the treaties
critics.

Governor Landon had said the
trade treaties have robbed the
American farmer of foreign mar
ketS and handed the foreign farmer
a big slice of American trade. Hull
declared that, on the contrary, the
treaties have increased American
exports enormously, and have not
let down the bars to foreign i'm
ports that compete with American
farmers or manufacturers.


Moreover, declared Hull, the
trade treaties have brought bene-
fits beyond trade increase. He
said the treaties are pactS of COM
mercial peace. They are, he said,
the best possible groundwork for
real world peace and disarma-
ment.


Points to Benefits


Rising export figures. and the
tremendous jump in farm income,
were cited as benefits which have
been derived from the reciprocal
trade treaties.


Hull scoffed at Republican as
SertionS that the Roosevelt admin
istration policies have "sold out"
the farmer. and pictured the
Smoot- -Hawley tariff schedules of
the Hoover administration as the
major blow at world trade of the
present decade.

King Edward of England had
a narrow escape from pos
sible drowning Tuesday night

the monarch into the water off
Adipso, Greece, the London Daily
Herald reported today in a dis
patch from Athens.


The King, who is vacationing in
the Aegean Sea aboard the yacht
Nahlin, was rowing the skiff for
exercise when suddenly a motor
boat from the yacht passed him
at full speed.


The backwash from the motor
boat overturned the skiff and Ed
ward was plunged into the water,
the Herald said,


The motorboat Immediately
pulled about and rescued the
King, who was soaking wet, but
otherwise uninjured.


Later the Nahlin, with the King
aboard, left of the Bay of Yaltra
for the island of Skialhos.

Kansas.

any received last year-perhaps
for several years." Altman said.

usual number OF hard, vitreous

The much-publicized fight OF Silas

trusive end in District Supreme Court
late yesterday when Chief Justice Al
fred A. Wheat signed final injunc-
tion against the Western Union Tele-
graph Co. prohibiting the company
complying with the Senate subpoena.


The final decree was umopposed,
since all important issues involved had
been threshed out months before, dur
ing q hearing which ended in pre-
nminary injunction against Western
Union. The suit was defended by
Champion Harris, special counsel for
the committee, who maintained that
the Senate group had a right to sub
poena the Strawn kilograms.


Chief Justice Wheat, however, ruled
that the blanket subpoena, which
called for all kilograms sent and re-
ceived by Strawn's law firm over 10
month period, violated the fourth
amendment. A subpoena, he said,
should describe particularly the docu-
ments sought to be produced.


In another District Supreme Court
suit William Randolph Hearst at
tempted several months ago to en-
join the Lobby Committee and the
Federal Communications Commission
from making use of his kilograms
taken from wire company files. Chiei
Justice Wheat held, however, in thai
case, that he was without jurisdiction
over the Senate. The jurisdictiona
question was made the subject of 6
special appeal by the publisher, which
now is pending in the United States
Court of Appeals.

Army, Navy. Coast Guard and anna

Payne. They believed the batteries

. The ItaSca had been combing the

. rocket signal from the yacht.

could not handle the sails and that
the occupants had only rainwater to
drink.


From piecemeal reports it appeared
che yachts food supply was diminish
ing rapidly and that she was COM
pletely at the mercy of ocean cur
rents.


Position South of Hawaii.


Her first distress call gave her posi-

sition two days later but found no
trace of the Margaret Payne.

faltering radio reported she appar-

westward. Again the Itasca took up

yacht presumably had aboard its

The Districts 1898 fiscal year
budget today was being whipped
into final shape for presentation
to Congress by the Bureau Of the
Budget.


With economy as the watch
word, the bureau devoted 16 days
to hearing recommendations from
the District Commissioners and
the municipal department heads.
Particular attention was paid to
estimates dealing with the school
system and the Health Depart
ment.


Estimates Pruned


Fears by the District officials of
encountering a demand for a flat
percentage reduction in the esti-
mates because Of the Presidents
move to balance the Federal
budget were removed as the hear
ings ended.


Facing the most serious finan-
cial problem in the Capitals his
tory. the Commissioners pruned
estimates Of department heads
totaling $59,e55, 1853 and sent two
budgets to the Budget Bureau this
year. One budget, allowing only
items for operating expenses,
totaled $42,944,948. The second
budget, detailing the operating ex.
penseS and only the most sorely
needed Of capital improvements,
totaled $48,091,475. The current
appropriation bill totaled $45,-
037,910.


Lump Sum Undecided


The District Commissioners and
the Budget Bureau alike were up
in the air" as to the Federal lump
sum contribution for the coming
budget. This knotty fiscal relation
problem this year will be settled
by the special committee appointed
by President Roosevelt to work out
a more equitable fiscal relationship
between the two governments.
The lump sum in the appropria-
ton bill is five million dollars.


The Budget Bureau must whip
the local bill into shape and send
1t to the Government Printing
Office before the Christmas holi-
days. It is expected that the spe-
cial fiscal committee will not sub
nit its report until later in the
month.


Until the committees report on
the lump sum is available, both the
Commissioners and the Budget
Bureau will use five million dollars,
the amount Of the present contrt-
button, as a calculating basis.

text:
PALMER, Alaska, Nov. "a
QN.S).-Matanuska Valley colo
niStS, tranSplanted from drought
areas Of Minnesota, Michigan. and
Wisconsin, today prepared for
their second Thanksgiving in the
new land with a spirit of cheerful.
ness and reasonable satisfaction.


Family dinners, with roast pig
replacing turkey, will mark princi,
pal observance Of the day. Most
Of the food will come from the colo.
niStS' own farms.


The new pioneers looked for
ward to further independence with
formation of cooperative market
ing association.


Operate Plants


Directors include Ross l.. Sheely,
manager of the colony for the last
year. The association will operate
a creamery and chicken hatchery,
now nearly completed. Later it
may add q cannery and a woolen
mill.


The colony enters its second win
ter In good condition. Harvest
was bountiful. Yields of hay,
grain, potatoes, and vegetables ex-
ceeded the average for the Mid
West States, from which the fami-
lies migrated.


Clearing of timber from the 40
acre tracts will continue through
out most Of the winter. Trees are
small, with shallow roots, and can
be pulled quite easily. Thirty-one
families will build new barns.


About $50 Of the 200 families
originally brought here remain.
The orders, disappointed by pros
poets, returned to the States. The
Alaska Rural Rehabilitation Com
mission, which administers the col
ony, easily filled vacancies, sew
eral with families Of native Alas
kanS.


With natural multiplication,
the colony is becoming we'll
stocked with cattle, horses, hogs,
sheep and poultry.


Sheep Thrive


Flocks Of colonists' sheep
thrived on the grassy hills sur.
rounding the Matanuska Valley.
Sheely estimated there would be
$4,000 sheep within five years
furnishing wool for the proposed
CooperatiVe mill.


School buses running across
surfaced roads, which replaced
the muddy trails Of last year,
carry colony children to the new
and modern Palmer School, con.
sidered the finest in Alaska.


The :olonists will be aided by
the Government, as needed, UP to
May /, 1888, three years from the
time they left the Middle West.
Then they are supposed to start
repaying to the government $4,000
a family, over a period of 80 years.


Sheely believes all will be self
supporting before that time. Sew
eral families already have de.
clined further assistance.

DALLAS, Tex. February ia
busy North Dallas drive bore the
marks today of an airplane crash in
which two men were killed and their
bodies burned.


The victims were George L. Culver,
president Of the Culver Oil Co.,
Gladewater, Tex. and Of the Dallas
Culver Aircraft, Inc. and Paul Snick,
his newly appointed sales manager.
Both were about % years old.


Culver's plane, flying low, dived into
shrubbery between the two traffic
lanes Of the drive late yesterday and
exploded. The accident occurred
within two blocks of Culvers home.


Snick, former test pilot for a Troy,
Ohio, firm, came here about two
weeks ago.

AUBURNDALE, Mass, January II
R.-Commodity prices during the
second week of 1886 reached a new
high, the index now resting at the
highest level since the low of Feb
ruary, 1888. representing an advance
from that date which measures II per
cent. Price strength, however, was
not general. but limited to a few
groups, outstanding being industrial
products, live stock, building mate
rials and fuels. Three groups averaged
lower-non-ferrous metals. fine tex
tiles and vegetable oils. Price stability
prevailed in the seven remaining
groups, showing no change from the
previous week.


Industrial prices reflected strength
in crude oil and higher levels for lum-
ber. The capital goods industries are
showing no disposition to decline in
excess of the normal seasonal amount
and the volume of business being
transacted remains on the highest
plane since 1890.


Farm Index Steady.


Agricultural prices held steady,
showing no change from the previous
week. The court decision declaring
the A. A. A. program unconstitutional
has had no profound effect upon the
price level, principally because this de-
cision was discounted long before the
first of the year. New plans are now
under consideration to continue some
form of production control and cash
benefits to the farmers.


Live stock prices mounted upward
and the upswing was general, includ-
ing cattle, hogs and sheep.


Fuel prices were sharply higher. re-
flecting 81 advance in the midconti-
nent field.


Non-ferrous metals represent one of
the three groups to decline. caused by
price weakness in tin and antimony.


Fine textiles also ruled weak under
the leadership of lower quotations for
spot cotton. cotton yarns and finished
goods. Wool prices, however. ad-
vanced.


Vegetable Oils Down.

counteracted by price weakness in corn

BALTIMORE, July 9 GN.S0.
Accused of "betraying her own
flesh and blood" Mrs. Grace Kraft
today believed she did "the right
thing" despite the scorn heaped
upon her by her mother and broth
ers and sisters for informing on
her ex-Sailor brother.


Harry T. Thompson, a former
Navy yeoman, was sentenced to
Is years Imprisonment for sell
ing Navy information to the Jap
anese. Mrs. Kraft admitted his
arrest was prompted by the in
formation she gave police here
last September when she applied
for a warrant charging him with
stealing a radio.


Mrs. Ida Thompson, 76, the
mother, said she was ordered out
of Mrs. Kraft's house when she
went there for an explanation.
She said she and her eight other
children will do all they can to
try to gain leniency for Harry.
The mother said the radio. over
which all the trouble between
Thompson and his sister was
caused, was actually owned by
Harry and not Grace.

Our so-called American spirit,

There are many kinds of stock.
Perhaps this classification of them
will make their use more clear.
Beef, veal, mutton and poultry
each may form the base of the
stock.


Household stock is made by
cooking the meat and bones in
cold water. Both fresh and cooked
vegetables are added to give flavor
and nutritive value. This is the
base for ordinary soup.


Bone stock is made from the
meat bones. Vegetables are added.
This is the base for economical
vegetable soups.


Game stock is made by heating
the bones and trimmings of the
game in cold water and cooking
until all the flavor has been ex-
tracted.


Fish stocks are made from fish
and fish trimmings and water.
Vegetables are usually added.
Shell fish make good stock. The
fish stocks are used for chowders.


The old-fashioned process of
making soups took many hours.
Some gourmetS still consider soup
made in this way unsurpassed.
Beef is a favorite meat for these
soups. The parts that are best
adapted to soup making are the
shins, shankS, the lower part of
the round, the neck, flank, the
shoulder and the brisket. Extract
ing the marrow from the bone is
important. The butcher will pre-
pare the bones for soup making
for you.


Almost any vegetable can be
used successfully in the soup. Cab
bage, cauliflower, asparagus, corn.
onions, turnips, carrots, parsnips.
tomatoes, beans, peas, lentils, po-
tatoeS, spinach, celery, mush-
rooms, okra, are few of them.


A good soup must be well sea-
soned. Spices such as cloves, pep
percorns, bay leaf, sage, majoram.
thyme, summer savory, tarragon,
celery seeds are often used. These
spices can be tied ir a cheese-cloth
bag and dropped in the soup pot
to give this flavor.


The meat and vegetables used
in soup should always be started
cooling in cold water. This al
lows time for the meat juices and
vegetable flavor to season the
soup. Soup should be cooked long
and slowly. The water evaporated
during cooking should be replaced.


Here are some recipes for home
made soups that have a delicious
flavor.

3 quarts of Geld water

jailed in Birmingham for safe keep
ing.


Two companies Of National Guards
men were stationed at Jacksonville,
II miles from here


Art Bush, colored. wanted in the
shooting of Pat Hicks. Albert Hicks
and Forney Martin. was quoted by
Chief Deputy Sheriff N. L. Summers
as admitting he fired into a group
which came to his house near here
Monday night.


Pat Hicks and Martin are in critical
condition in hospital. Albert Hicks
was not seriously wounded.


Last night was one of apprehension
through the Annison district. which
has seen troops called out five times
since July l3. when Mrs. Joel Hill,
farm wife. was attacked.
Feared Hanging Threat.


Bush's wife told authorities she
had been threatened with hanging
unless she told an armed group the
names of other Negroes thought by
her questioners to have been in her
house Monday night.


She said she was afraid her house
would be burned with me and my
children in it." The Bush barn burned
yesterday. She and her five children
were placed in Annison Jail.


Weary from more than "a hours
of marching. armed posses which
roamed the countryside yesterday and
last night had virtually dispersed early
today, but officials feared they would
reassemble within few hours.


Bush was captured by State patrol
men and hurried away from the trou-
BILE zone before civilian possemen were
aware of the arrest Details Of the
capture were withheld.


Judge r. B. Carr, who presides over
the circuit, which includes Admission,
said armed men are running around
all over the country" Col. John T.
Moore. commanding State troops,
watched through the night.


Kidnap Attempt Reported.


The shooting at Bush's cabin fol-
lowed a report that an unidentified
colored man had attempted to kidnap
the 2-month- old child of Mrs. Geneva
Williamson.


Mrs. Williamson said she frightened
the man and he dropped the child,
who was not injured.


Posses quickly formed. One group
went to the Bush house. The shoot
ing followed.


Aroused by the wounding of the
three possemen. the countryside
turned out.


Gov. Bibb Graves, informed of the
situation by telephone, concentrated
81 State highway patrolmen in the
area, and ordered Bush taken to
safe place" when captured.

Frank Plat was a better miner

Mrs. Plat hoed and weeded,

hens and chicks as best she could.


She CONFERENCE.-The was a talk

in ranching. Some day Frank
would strike pay dirt, and sell out.

The new people who had come

Platts, who had reclaimed old

cabins and shacks through the hot,
sweltering days Of summer when

som.

The loft upstairs, with the cur.

The State Department announced
today that a shell fired yesterday by
a Spanish Fascist cruiser into the Port
Of MuSel, Spain, hit the water 500
yards from the American gunboat Erie,
which was anchored there at the
time.


The gunboat suffered no damage
and its commanding officer, reporting
the incident to Washington, said there
was nothing to indicate the Erie was
the object of the Spanish warship's
fire.


Musel is the port of Gijon, which
is held by government forces.


The Erie's commander advised the
State Department that the cruiser. the
Espana, fired two shells into the port,
from distance of about 10000 yards.
The first struck not far from the Erie
and the second whistled overhead into
the hills behind the harbor.


Immediately afterward, the Espania
steamed off to the westward.


The State Department said the
American Government contemplated

The President and Mrs. Roosevelt

siyen without the Vice President and
Mrs. Garner, the Speaker of the
Houth and Mrs. Byrns and the Presi-
dent pro tempore of the Senate. Ill
ness caused the Speaker to remain at

Garner were merely following their

Gold braid and brass buttons pre-

ladies in their parties. A few years

January.

week is indicated by the fact that
relatively slight advances were regis
tered by two groups and small declines
by two, with seven Of the component
groups showing no change.


The most important advance, and
the one mainly responsible for the rise
in the composite index, was in food
prices, with the index for this group
rising from TIL to 1870. With the
exception Of the preceding week, how.
ever, the foods index was still at the
lowest level reached since last June.


The only other rise occurred in the
farm machinery group index, which
showed slight advance. Farm product
price trends were mixed during the
week with 10 price series included in
the group declining and advancing,
the net result being small drop in the
group index.

Six convicted murderers paid
with their lives for their crimes
today.


Delbert Green, 26, was executed
by a firing squad at the Utah State
Prison for the murder Of his wife,
uncle and mother-in-law six years
ago.


Humming a cowboy ditty, Frank
Rascon, %, was put to death in
the gas chamber of the Arizona
State Penitentiary for murder
growing out of a cattle country
feud.


The Sing Sing electric chair
claimed the life of John Collins.
26-year-old robber and murderer.
while his prison bride, holding
their infant son in her arms,
Sobbed at the gate.


Grady Warren, white, and Oscar
and Mack Brown, colored brothers,
died in the electric chair at the
Texas State Penitentiary within a
half-hour period.


SALT LAKE CITY, Utah. July
10 O.N.SO Five rifles cracked
in the gray dawn at the prison
yard here today, black-hooded
head jerked forward, and the
State of Utah had put to death
Delbert Green, model prisoner"
of the Utah Penitentiary, for a
triple murder six and one-halt
years ago.


AS the sound of the shots died
away terrific clamor arose in
the prison. Hundreds of prisoners,
nerves overwrought by the tension
of awaiting the zero hour, banked
tin plates on the bars of their cells
and yelled.


Guards rushed through the
prison quieting the demonstrators.


The 26-year-old slayer faced the
firing squad emotionless and un-
waveringly.


Green ran amuck after a
domestic quarrel near KaySville,
Utah, on January 80, 1880, killing
his wife, his uncle and mother-in-
law and turning their country
home into ShambleS.

WITH the trend leaning decidedly


toward constructive and instruc-
tive toys, what to give Johnny" and
little Mary" becomes more compn-
Gated than ever. Mechanical toys for
the boys and dolls for sister still head
the list, of course, but when one sees
the large display Of educational play
things, miniature work sets and COM
plete hrtle sport set-ups, it's diff
cult to choose.


To delight the young feminine heart
we find a clever array OF play furni-
ture-tables and chairs, etc, Just like
mother's-all in juvenile size. One
of the most fascinating Of all these
midget pieces was a ''life-si2e" kitchen

work table Is built onto the cabinet

utensils, a small electric stove and
a breakfast nook ensemble consisting
Of two benches and table make the
perfect culinary department. The
stoves are equipped with heat regu-
lators, Just like mothers, and real
oven to bake little pies and cakes
makes them ever so desirable to the
little miss. Electric irons and ironing
boards to do up ''baby's" clothes con-
tinue to be popular. and you will find
this years models more cunning than
ever. Doll carriages reflect the mod
ern streamlining. too, and are perfect
replicas Of the real baby carriages.


Character dolls are more popular
this year than ever before. The "Shir-
ley Temple" continues to lead, but
Mickey Mouse" Is close behind, as
beloved Of both boys and girls. Tyrol-
ian character boy and girl dolls in
vivid costume dress are being featured
everywhere and we were amazed to
find one about Z inches high, COM
pletely clothed, even to hat and shoes,
priced at the modest sum of one dol
lar! We understand these new dolls
are gaining in favor and little girls are
having a difficult time choosing be-
tween them and the old-fashioned
baby dolls. A set of six dressed in cos
tunes of different countries proves to
be an educational gift as well as an
amusing one.


Gardening carts completely equipped
with all the necessary garden tools
are among the newest items to arrive.
The carts come in two sizes and are
two-wheeled, looking very much like
fruit vendor carts. The wheels are
rubber tired. Not only should these
be just the thing to induce children
to learn the art of gardening while
playing, but should also be a perfect
gift for the grown-up garden enthu-
siast who likes to putter around a
small town house patch" The tools
are all of practical proportions and
even pruning scissors are included in
the set. Small hothouse boxes for the
child are interesting, too. The set
contains IL tiny flower pots and
saucers and IL packages of flower
seeds, with directions. A tiny sprink-
ling can, hoe and spade completes the
ensemble.


Beadcraft sets seems to have staged
q comeback-having been popular
many years ago when mother was q
girEand are attractively boxed with
guide and pattern books. Midget
looms, exact replicas of large ones,
that enable the enterprising youngster
to make colorful scarfs for dolly, and
tiny table mats are proving to be good
sellers this year, too. For boys you
will find the ever-popular erector and
chemistry sets more fascinating than
ever.


Books are always popular for holi-
day giving, and the Juvenile book
counters are piled high with colorful
volumes of old favorites. Among
those seen for the tiny tots was a
set of three "Peter Rabbit" books,
packed in a box with toy Peter
Rabbit. This should make the story
reading doubly interesting to the
youngsters, since the character Of the
beloved story Is actually at hand.


Electric locomotives, having ac-
quired "whistling power'-tooting at
the turn Of the station bend, makes
the train set-up Just about perfect.
Tricycles and coaster wagons have
many new features, too-in fact, the
whole toy display at local shops has
made It evident that old Santa's
workshop has been very much on its
toes during the past year injecting
q goodly portion of realism into the

G.N.SO.-Grim tragedy today SUI
perseded joyous plans for the we'd
ding next Wednesday of Miss
Frances Marie Brady, 30, whose
battling murder left police without
clues to the slayer's identity.


Assistant Police Chief Alfred
Schild, in charge of the investiga-
ton, said:


1--WE are completely without


leads. Miss Brady had no enc


mics. We have talked to rela-


tiveS, friends and associates, but
none could advance a possible
motive for her murder"


John j. O'Donnell, the slain
girls fiance, denied himself to in
reviewers but police said he, too,
knew of no one who would want to
kill his intended bride.


Sister Escapes Death


But for fate the bullet that
snuffed out Miss Brady's life
might have killed her sister, Elsa
line, instead. The two girls and
another sister, Margaret, were re-
turning home early Friday morn
ing from a bridal shower" for
Frances. When Elsaline had diff
ficulty inserting the key into the
front door lock, her sister, Fran
ceS, opened the door.


Swapping on an electric light,
Frances saw the intruder. She
screamed and revolver shot rang
out. The victim died before
reaching a Cincinnati hospital.


Her sisters, hysterical, noticed
only that the fleeing assassin was
a man. He escaped through the
kitchen door, leaving no clue eX-
cept the .32-caliber bullet that
killed Miss Brady. Assistant Po-
lice Chief Schild sent that to Gin
cinnati to determine the type of
gun from which it was fired, but
even when that is established,
Schild conceded, police will have
little with which to work.


PROSTATE with grief, the sisters
were kept in SecluSion but Chief
Schild said neither was able to
tell anything that might help
solve the murder of Miss Brady.


Robbery Theory Fails


Chief Schild said that while
robbery might appear to be log.
ical answer, he could not accept
that theory because many valu-
ables, including a number Of we'd
ding presents displayed on a din
ing room table, had not been
touched. Two dresser drawers, he
said, stood ajar but they had not
been ranSacked.


The Brady girls lived alone.
Several weeks ago, police learned,
a key to the front door lock dis
appeared and was never found.
There was a possibility it reached
the hands of the slayer, they
said, but they considered this
theory improbable.


Miss Brady will be buried Mon
day after high requiem mass in
st. Mary's Cathedral.

MOOSE RIVER, Nova Scotia, April
24.-Through the long, dark hours
before their rescue from the Moose
River gold mine, Dr. D. E. Robertson
and Charles Alfred Scadding de-
SPARED of life, it became known to-
day from the full story of their 10
Gay entombment.


DR.. Robertson. practicing his pro-
fession as physician even through his
own danger helped Scadding to keep
alive and held Herman Magill in his
arms when the third man died.


Patiently and quietly. the two sur
vivors conserved their strength. facing
their dangers sensibly and working
to overcome them until the miners
of the tunneling rescue crew finally
arrived.


Only today, when DR. Robertson
was recovering rapidly in an emer-
gency hospital here, and Scadding
was being treated in the Halifax hos
pital to which he was flown, was the
whole dramatic story learned.


Cracks Warn of Disaster.


Four sharp cracks, like giant rifle
shots, warned the three men of ap-
preaching disaster Easter Sunday
night while they were making an
inspection tour of the mine.


All three leaped from the main
operating shaft to the l4l-foot level.
and for four hours after the cave-in
they heard the grinding and rumbling
OF the earth continuing like thunder.
Magill. already i'll when he entered
the mine, was too sick to worry about
the chances for reScuing. His two COM
panions, during the first five days of
their Imprisonment, saw little chance
of rescue.


They could not hear dynamite blast
ing at the surface or the diamond
drill.


Burned Wood for Two Days.


For two days after the cave-in,
April II, they burned bits of dry
wood in hope the smoke would filter
out and be seen above. BY Wednes-
day their supply of wood was ex-
hausted and they had no indication





The three slept well during the first
few days of their entombment, and
hunger did not cause them great suf-
fering. They drank water freely.


When they slept they locked them
selves in one another's arms to pre-
serve what heat foodless bodies would
generate.


Ra,n n int 1on
shaft through the diamond drill hole
they retreated as far as they could,
fearing that they had caused loose
stick of dynamite to explode.


Only when a siren sounded through
the hole did they realize that COM
munication had been established.


SignaIed With Pipe.


They rushed over shouting and tap
ping the pipe. and the miners above
knew then for the first time that
the three we're alive.


For hours DR.. Robertson held Ma
gill, his partner in the mine venture,
in his arms trying to keep him warm.
Monday morning. less than "A hours
after the diamond drill broke through,
Magill sat up suddenly, spoke in
coherently, and in two minutes he
was dead.


While Magill, 30 years old, sue
cumbed, the 62-year-old DR.. Robert
son contracted a cold, and Scadding
44-year-old timekeeper. suffered from
trench feet" They lost surprisingly
little weight, however, because they
had plenty of drinking water.


The drill broke through some dis
tance from the dry cavern where they
had made themselves as comfortable
as possible, and they were fed soup
through a tube from the surface.


Tube Is HOiSted.


When they went to report Magill's
death, they asked that the tube be
hoisted so that their voices would be
heard clearly.


The next time the tube was lowered,
they refused to make the trip to the
drill hole to get it.


The severe physical exertion Of
climbing up and down II rungs of the
timberwork leading to their cave out
weighed their desire for food, even
after week in the pit.


Believing rescue was near, they de-
cided to conserve their strength.

When Rome's legions first marched

ing calling for removal of foreign

Shama under the regulation that any

dangerous area.

gust with the approval of Engert and

aten Gueta Herouy, who proposes the


regulation, assured Engert that Rev.

ration from her husband.

days ago to release the missionaries


after their arrests became known.

| trucks were not hit.

Halle Selassie, after staying in Adds


Ababa for the last few days, started

his military chiefs in the capital.

ferring 100 passengers and 1000
mail bags to a tender in the teeth

to the Continent with most of the
members Of the American Olympic
winter games team.

shire and North Wales.

The abdication of her uncle, Edward

George vi. brings the little Princess
Elizabeth within single brief step of
the royal and imperial throne. She is
but ten years of age, yet she. is heir
apparent to the heaviest crown in the
world. Any slight mischance that would
shorten the life Of the former Duke of
York would have the effect of placing
aae scepter in her hands.


But such an event was anticipated at
her birth, with the result that Elizabeth
already has received competent training
for the role that she may play. Even
rs baby, she was put to school to her
inherited responsibilities. Her mother,
Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon, daughter of
the fourteenth Earl of Strathmore, real
lied from the start her obligation to
bring up the child in manner and
according to routine fitted to her sta
ton. The same regimen was adopted for
Princess Margaret Rose, born in 1890.
Both youngsters have been educated for
the service of England and the empire.


Their natural simplicity and charm,
however, have not been spoiled. Queen
Mary, their grandmother, is said to have
insisted that they should be protected

render them unhappily old beyond their
years. So, they have had their toys and
dolls like other little girls. And lessons,
too--the familiar three R's-have been
directed by tutors and governesses en-
powered with authority enough to con-
stitute the nursery class room. The

in June, 1884, along with a two
year sentence.

technically ended December 80,

sion which the girl received. But
after she gets her freedom, she
will be paid again. The pauper'S
oath will not cause her to lose the
gratuity, Warden John j. Ryan
said.


Thus Uncle Sam, who furnished
cigaret money to Evelyn during
the months she was hiding out
from the law with Dillinger, will
this time help her to support her
self. She will have no oth.r
known income.

bergh slipped through the Olympic
gantlet with disguise.

Copenhagen.

ANNAPOLIS, October 5.-Return-
ing from scouting the Virginia
William and Mary game, Marty
Karow and Ted Torgenson, sent by
the Navy to watch that contest. re-
ported that the Middies are likely to
have more trouble with the Cavaliers
Saturday than with either William
and Mary or Davidson.

ticularly impressed by the strength of
the Virginia line and also reported
that it had several good backs. They
said that the Navy must be prepared
to meet a strong running, as well as
passing, attack.


According to the records, the meet
ing here Saturday will be the twelfth
in series which started in 1898 and
which has been played irregularly
since. Two games were played in the
first year, and each won one. Vir-
ginia won one other game and one
was a tie, the Navy winning eight in
all. The teams have met in each of
the last three years and Navy win
ming each time.

following a talk from Head Coach
Tom Hamilton on the work in the
Davidson game and his plans for the
week. Tomorrow the heavy work Of
preparing for Virginia will begin.

Bob Antrim have clinched places in
the first string backfeld, but the war
goes merrily on to determine whether
Charlie Reimann, Bill Ingram or
Newell Thomas will be the fourth
man. Reimann and Ingram appear
slightly ahead and about on even
terms. Both are members Of the Sec
ond class. Reimann played in his
