Her head snapped up. She stiffened.
That was Bill-Bill Torger calling the
break! 1t was the way he always called.
Nervous, worried. But it couldn't be.
Bill was on the ocean. He was going
to the Olympics. She forced her hands
rigidly before her. Her toes pointed
and her arms fexed at the elbows.


Her eyes were wide, now - staring
into the light that lifted to meet her.
She knew what was coming. She'd
missed "a voice had tricked her. 1t
wasn't Bill. That voice was in her
mind. Bill had been right. She needed
him. She'd always needed him there to
call the break.


And then she hit.


The water was a solid thing that
beat at her breast and throat. A fare
Of light and she was past the surface.
Her hip slammed against the bottom
of the tank, and then the throwback
caught her and tossed her erect.


Thunder roared in her ears. The
crowd was applauding perfect dive.
White light poured into the tank and
she gripped the steel edge. Her feet
found the bottom and she stood there,
staring into the light.


Mice work, partner"


1t was Howard He had started up

II made it," she whispered.
Howard - Imade it."


why. of course you did. That
break was right on the PIN"


But who called it?" she asked.


His hands slid upward along the
ladder rails, but for an instant he
leaned toward her and smiled.


who? That partner of mine -
Madge keystone" There was more
than pride in his eyes. IAN she needed
was someone to trust her. Just that -
sweetheart"


She watched him swinging upward
into the night. And strangely, the
night had become warm and friendly.

the lightsv"


The drum answered her. 1t laughed
at a professional who couldn't dive
into light. 1t laughed at Madge Key
stone who liked silk and soft things. 1t
laughed until Madge cried out again
and waved her arms.


And suddenly darkness swept down
upon her. The lights were off and she
was alone in night-flled sky. Alone?
1t was more than that. Madge felt the
blackness grow to immensity. She was
so small - a speck that lived in a sea
of light. She couldn't find the ground
- the tank - anything. There was
nothing but night. 1t had texture and
body. She felt it crowding. wrapping
about her in soft folds. And family. as
though from a great distance, she
heard the drum.


"Dive," it said. "Dioe, dire, dire.


She leaned forward. The lights were
on again but she didn't care. She was
diver-aprofessional. Howard trusted
her. He knew she could do it. She had
to dive. She leaned further into the
wind and thought again of his instruc-
tions, the first rule of the two-and-a-
half: Lift - look - spinr


1t sounded easy. She'd done it
hundred times, a thousand. But there
was no use trying to convince herself
she was not afraid. Not here. Not in
the night. Maybe she'd always been
afraid. And Bill was right - she
needed him. She bit her lower lip be-
tween her teeth. Lift - look - spin!
- and if she missed?


Her eyes were staring off into black
ness and she tried not to think of the
tank below. Lift She forced upward.
Her feet left the platform and she
whirled into space. LooM That was to
allow for the split second of inertia at
the top of the dive. Spin! Her head
went down; she caught her knees and
drew them tightly beneath her chin.


Asplash of light swept by. That was
the ground - the food lamps. How
ard was there. He was smiling. con-
fident. He trusted her. Darkness! She
was swinging around to the top of the
turn. Her eyes fought with the night.
Bill was out there-out in the night.
And he was going away. Far away.
She thrust forward. One turn was past
and now she was rolling into the
second. Light! A binding flash that
streaked past like comets tail. 1t
spread. and fused with the darkness.
And suddenly Madge knew she was
lost.


She was turning. spinning, falling
through space. Her arms clamped
tighter about her knees. She Rugged
them to her and closed her eyes. All
sense of direction was gone - all
sense of timing. She was lost in a world
of motion. and rushing wind, and a
drum that rolled and rolled. Nothing
could stop her now.


Nothing. No one was there to help
her. No one realized she needed help.
Howard trusted her. He'd be smiling
that suave, confident smile of the pro-
fessional. And suddenly that smile
would 60. His face would tense and
he'd cry out. But it would be too late.
He couldn't help her then. No one
could help her, no one -

To the Editor Of The Star:


The thousands of renters in Washing
ton are anxiously awaiting to see If Mrs.
Norton will follow up her attack on the
high rents in Washington. Our rents
are advancing, and especially to Gov
eminent clerks, many of whom must
leave their own small-town homes, where
they could rent comfortable apartment
for half Of what they must pay here.


The Government owes the unfortunate
people an opportunity to make decent
living, and if the thousands of young
Government clerks whose parents are
independently established in comfortable
homes and who are able to pay high
rents were refused the thousands of
jobs they now hold here in Washing

SO acute.


But these bloodsuckers in the form of
rental agents. owners and renters who
subrent are taking advantage Of the
present crisis.


This question has been before Con-
gresS long enough to have decided action
and results, but last year, after Congress
agitated the question and did absolutely
nothing, the rents advanced, and this
Fall thousands of Government clerks,
who could barely make buckle and tongue
meet, were forced to pay from S. to $40
more for apartments.


The situation demands that all rents,
apartments, rooms and houses, be reduced
10 per cent on or by February Is, with
no long g-drawn-out red tape argument
concerning the renting conditions that
are now preventing large per cent Of
Washington citizens from having the
proper food and clothing for their
families, thereby increasing Ill health,
disease, unhappiness and bitterness.
Their minds are ready and ripe for the

ing them while our Government is feed
ing, educating and employing these same
treacherous and un-Americanized for
eigners and our own countrymen are
sinking to the lowest phase of life.


Our thoughtful citizens are weary and
disgusted with procrastination on the
part of those who are paid well to pro-
tect our property and our lives.


Does Germany. France, italy or Russia
permit foreigners who are not self-sup-
porting to enter their country, or allow
undesirable and dangerous ones to re-
main there? We can learn some good
lessons from these countries which would
make our country safer for democracy.


A. L. BATTLE.

VATICAN CITY, December 27
Sunday Pope Plus slept uneasily
early this morning as pain frequently
aroused him, wel1-informed sources
reported today, after prelates' hope
for the pontiff's recovery had dwin-
died with reliable reports paralysis had
extended over his entire left side.


The Pope before attempting to go
to sleep recited the Rosary with his
secretaries.


Doctors remained within call, it
was said, and nurses maintained q
constant vigil.


The circulatory congestion, accom-
panied by old-age complications, was
declared to have made the holy
fathers left arm useless. The 79-
year-old Pope was not able to move
his legs yesterday. authoritative
sources said.


Osservatore Romano, Official Vatican
newspaper, described the pontii as
suffering from piercing, insistent
spasms of pain"


A critical turn within the next few
days would not be surprising, some
prelates said sadly. Many abandoned
all hope for the aged ecclesiastic's re-
covery from the af1iction which sent
him to bed three weeks ago.


Cardinal Paceli Visitor.


Only Eugenio Cardinal Pacelli,
papal secretary of state, was allowed
inside the sickroom with DR.. Amanti
Milani, the pontiff's physician, who
was said to be in almost constant at.
tendance on his patient.


Highly important church problems
were left pending or were settled by
the Pope's subordinates without con-
sultation with the invalid.


Pope Plus slept much of yesterday
after awakening from a restless sleep.
He listened to mass said in the study
adjoining his bed room and then
mapped throughout the morning.
Cardinal Pacelli visited him around
| noon.


Reliable sources disclosed the holy
father recently lost q front tooth but
is unable to stand the strain of having
his dentist treat him. This loss, il
was reported. interfered with his pro-
nunciation during his radio address
Thursday.

Some tightening of his burden was
given the Ill pontiff by news of chill
dren's prayers being said for him.
Osservatore Romano declared he
even laughed feebly at letter from

| which said:


"I wish you were Louis and the
Pope 80 ! could bless you because I
love you"


The Pope read the child's letter
several times, said the newspaper
which has sponsored q crusade Of
children's prayers for the pontiff's re.
covery.

longing to the crews of two

rived from Spain revOlted and

Land batteries Immediately.
stopped progress of the ships,
and the crews were captured.


"The attempt caused indig-
nation among the land and sea
forces. Lisbon and the entire
country are calm"

eight wounded when the sloop

NEW YORK, May 9.-Despite the
cloudy foreign outlook, buying sup
port got behind the stock market to-
day and pushed up leading issues frac-
tions to 2 or more points.


Although there was some last-min-
ute proft-taking, the close was firm.
The upturn was accomplished In the
dullest session since last June. Trans
fers we're around $4,000 shares.


Among the principal gamers were
j. I. Case. Du Pont. Philip Morris,
Continental Can, United States Steel.
Bethlehem, General Motors, Allied
Chemical, Chrysler, Sears, Roebuck;
Western Union. American Smelling.
Anaconda, Santa Fe, New York Cen
tral and Southern Pacific.


There was a run on Hupp Motors
for an advance of nearly a point fol-
lowing announcement that the COM
pany would resume plant operations
which were suspended last year.


With the exception of French OBJ
legations, which fell sharply, bonds
improved. Wheat steadied after its
relapse of yesterday. Foreign curren-
cies were somewhat irregular.


Uppermost in the minds Of the
trading fraternity was the French
financial crisis, with the possibility
of a cut in the franc, when the new
"Leftist' government takes over.


Banking quarters were not so sure
that downward revaluation of this
monetary unit would be resorted to
Immediately, but there were some who
thought an embargo might be slapped
on gold exports if the flight of funds
from the republic continues.


The weekend closing of the Bourse
brought a respite for French author
tiles, who issued reassuring statements
regarding the fiscal situation. Paris
bankers also agreed to refuse loans Of
francs for speculative purposes. The
French currency was steady in terms
Of the dollar.

FORT BELVOIR, Va, January g.
Three men and dog were waiting to-
day for tug to pull their gravel barge
from the middle of the Potomac,
where they have been virtually
stranded for nearly two weeks.


Ice which locked the craft like a
ship in polar regions has disappeared.
but the barge has no power and must
wait for tow.


A skiff driven by an outboard motor
went out yesterday from the Bureau
of Fisheries station here, taking food
and coal oil for the group.


The provisions were the first to
reach the barge Sidney since New
Year day. That was the only time
courage faltered in the hearts Of the
men out there. Jagged chunks of ice,
like concrete slabs, stove a hole in the
barge. Water was coming in in a
stream big around as your arm," &C
cording to Cecil Wright. captain.


Plod Over Ice.


Wright and half his crew. Ben Huf-
ham of Wilmington, N. c., set out to
walk across the ice for help, their only
chance in their desperate plight.
George Rolf, who gives his address as
mostly anywheres," and Spook, the
dog, stayed aboard, anxiously watch
ing their shipmates as they slithered
across the frozen river


It was a long walk and bitter cold.
but the ice held, and after plodding
more than a mile and half Wright
and Huffman reached a house little
to the north of the deserted amuse-
ment park at Marshall Hall. There
they telephoned for help. A Navy rug
came the next day. smashing its way
through the ice and bringing food, in
cluding chickens, and repair materials


Meanwhile Wright and Huffman had
walked back to the Sidney. The water
was coming in faster now. They
hacked hole in the ice and patched
the old wooden hull with rough planks.
A wheeling boiler was fired up and
pumps threw the icy food back into
the river. That did the trick till the
Navy tug came.

noon he screamed hoarsely, attracting
the attention of his mother, Mrs.

dinner.

administered artificial respiration. The
rescue squad was called, and after
working over Mary. the firemen took
her to Casualty Hospital, where she
was pronounced out of danger last
night. although suffering from sub
mersion and shock.

baby In the tub before going down.
stairs to put some potatoes on the
stove for dinner. A few moments
later she heard the scream from the
second floor.

7-month-old son, George Ralph Davis,
when the infant died Of heat prostra-

Two burlap bags, similar to that

last Wednesday while she was
searching for her small son. In
her anxiety over the boys absence,
Mrs. Brennan said, she forgot to
notify authorities at the time.


Weighted With Stones


Authorities believed the bags
discovered today may have con-
tanned the torso Of the slain
woman. Both sacks had been
weighted with stones.


Victor Davidson, 10, Of Quincy,
said that he saw a torso afloat
in Rock Island Cove while he
was picking up driftwood. Police
were dredging there. They said
they not only expected to find
the missing parts of the slain

of Lyons, whom they believe was

NEW YORK. February 1.-Malor
commodities successfully eluded the
imitation virus that was widely credited
with motivating the weeks rise in stock
prices.


The Associated Press commodity
index dropped ST during the week to
1851.


Tumbling prices for the heavily
weighted farm products-hogs, cattle,
cotton, wheat-overbalanced the fact
that gains outnumbered declines IL
to 8. Fifteen prices were unchanged
for the week.


Live Stock Down.


Hog and cattle quotations swept
downward as consumer resistance to
higher prices continued to make itself
felt in the bidding at the yards. A
slight advance in lambs was felt to be
of slight consequence as the price re-
manned within the narrow range that
has prevailed for the past month.


Wheat continued lower with the
visible world supply apparently deemed
more important than the poorer-than-
expected quality of the Canadian crop
Oats also were somewhat depressed al
though corn and rye eked out minor
advance.


Cotton slumped precipitously on
Friday as traders became apprehensive
of the Governments intention regard
ing the disposal of its collateral for
loans to farmers.


Food prices continued the advancing
tendency of last week, with eggs, cocoa.
coffee and lard sharing the spotlight.
Flour alone showed weakness, dropping
10 cents a barrel.


The costs of the commodities used
directly in industry were steady in the
main, although bituminous coal and
burlap dropped bit

industry is maintaining its recent high

After a four-year battle for posses
sion of her daughter, now 8, during
which she recently was arrested in
New York on kidnapping charge, Mrs.
Nettie Madigan, 1914 Connecticut ave-
nue., was back at home today with the
little girl safe In her custody.


Five days ago Justice Joseph w. Cox
of District Supreme Court, who in 1882
gave the child, Betty Lyvia Lugaresi,
to her father, Terzo Lugaresi, retired
member of the Marine Band, ordered
the child transferred to her mothers
custody. He authorized Mrs. Madigan,
remarked since her divorce from Luga-
resi-. to take the child forthwith, wher-
ever she could be found. Lugaresi did
not appear at the hearing.


Mrs. Madigan Immediately left for
New York and located the little girl
in the Bronx. The child was sick and
Mrs Madigan forcibly took her from
Lugaresi and started for Washington.


Under Arrest for While.


The father, however, notified police,
who blocked all outlets from the city.
Mrs. Madigan was arrested and
charged with kidnapping, but finally
effected her release after she had dis
played the decree of the Washington
court.


Lugaresi was awarded q divorce
November 10, 1882, after a bitterly
contested trial here and was given
custody Of the child. Two efforts by
the mother in District Supreme Court
to regain the little girl and one hearing
before Juvenile Court Judge Fay Bent
ley ended unsuccessfully for her.


On December "a last the mother
filed another petition in District Su-
preme Court, through Attorney Jean
M. Boardman, stating she had mar
ried Joseph Madigan and had a suit
able home for Betty. She said further
that Lugaresi was neglecting the child.


Lugaresi Gets Order.


While this petition was still pending
Lugaresi obtained an order from the
court permitting him to remove his
daughter from the District for three
weeks to visit his sister in Boston.


At the recent hearing Mrs. Madigan
told the court he had failed to return,
although the three weeks period had
expired.

opinion handed down by Federal Judge

Granting permanent injunction to

Regional Action Dismissed.


While the injunction was granted

venting it from further investigating
union complaints in the power strike
here, Judge Boynton dismissed similar
action filed against the Regional Labor
Board.


Judge Boynton's decision stated the
utility company has shown "irrepar-
able injury and damage" occasioned by
the filing of National Labor Board
complaints of unfair labor practices, {"
and that the company has no "ade-
quate remedy at law


Based on Supreme Court Ruling.


The decision was based partially on
the United States Supreme Courts
outlawing of the Guffey coal act.


Judge Eoynton ruled that the Fed
eral District Court here had jurisdic-
ton over the case and that the "enact-
ment of the Wagner act exceeded the
powers vested in it (Congress) under
either the interstate commerce clause
or commerce clause or any other clause

WYTHEVILLE, Va. May 30
Edith Maxwell's attorneys will carry
her celebrated fight for freedom be-
fore the Virginia Supreme Court OF
Appeals here Tuesday.


Attorney General A. p. Staples will
represent the State in opposing a new
trial for the school teacher who was
sentenced to Is years in prison for
the murder of her father, Trigg Max
well, village blacksmith at Pound.
Wise County, last July 81.


She contends the only blows she
inflicted were with slipper, when
her father attempted to whip her and
she resisted.


Circuit Judge H. A. w. Skeen has
twice refused to set aside the verdict
Of the Cumberland mountain jury that
convicted Miss Maxwell last Novem-
Der. The Supreme Court consented
March 10 to review the case.


Charge Is Continued.


Meanwhile. murder charge against
Mrs. Anne Maxwell, jointly indicted
with her daughter, has been con-
tinued.


The seven judges also will hear
q plea that Miss Maxwell be released
under bond from the Jail, where she
has been confined since her arrest
nearly a year ago. Judge Skeen has
consistently declined to grant bail.


Defense attorneys alleged 10 errors
on the part of the trial court, one
of which was the exclusion of women
from the jury under Virginia law. The
latter point was made after the Vir-
ginia branch of the National Woman's
Party engaged an attorney in the case.


Miss Maxwell was arrested after her
father died in their cabin at Pound,
and went on trial on November l8,
1885. She, her mother, and her young
sister Mary Katherine testified that
the father was drunk and had told his
wife she would have to leave the
home.


Returned About Midnight.


The defendant said she returned
from a date about midnight, and her
father seized and attempted to beat
her. He had a knife in his hand.
but dropped it. she said, and caught
her roughly by the hair. Stumbling
over a chair in the darkened room.
she snatched a high-heeled slipper
from the room and hit him several
times on the head, she testified.


Mrs. Maxwell said when he fell
against a meat block on the back
porch later she assumed the fall killed
him.


ITS hell when you can't even whip
your own child" Edith quoted her
father as saying during the struggle.


Commemorative Attorney Fred B.
Greear put witnesses on the stand who
testified that Maxwell was not drunk
short time before the family fight,
that Edith had been heard to threaten
her father on several occasions, and
that she had been heard to say she
would laugh If she saw him laying
out dead"

WITH THE ITALIAN ARMY IN
Adds ABABA, May 8.-Young Ethi-
opian children gave the Fascist salute
to all Europeans today as the Italian
army OF occupation cleaned up the
desolated former imperial capital Of
Ethiopia.


The youngsters were encouraged to
do so by priests of both the Mussul-
man and Coptic Christian religions
who promised to aid Italian authori-
ties in bringing peace.


As order began to prevail after the
riotng and looting which followed
Emperor Halle Selassie's flight last
Saturday, Italian officers said they
found evidence that the pillaging Of
the capital was carried out system
attcally.


Natives reported the looters moved
from store to store and from house to
house under the command Of Ethi-
opian officers, raiding establishments,
soaking them with fuel and firing
them.


The imperial library, ministerial
quarters and other buildings adjoin-
ing the imperial palace were burned
to the ground.


Among the foreign missions, the
Turkish Legation suffered most, being
sacked and burned. The Turkish
Minister escaped with his life. but his
sister was missing and two servants
dead.

Two well-known farms here have

Mountain View, home of the Bolts

days, was sold by the owner, Lewis
Browning, to Raymond Quaintance

fertile land, has an interesting old
residence from which a panoramic
view of the Blue Ridge Mountains

the ancestral home of the Bolts fam
lily, prominent in early Culpeper his
tory. and came into the Browning
family through marriage. Until now
1t had never belonged to any one else.


The Quaintance farm of. 335 acres,
near Culpeper, being a part of the
older Burton tract, has just been sold
TO z. Turpin Willis. who, with this
latest addition to his already large
holdings, will be one of the largest
landowners in Culpeper County.
Willis. who owns historic Rother-
wood, near Culpeper, having recently
acquired the Stonesiffer farm Of sew
eral hundred acres, which was added
10 the Perry place. purchased some

ance land also.

AMES, Iowa, January 1.-THE re-
vived proposal for soil conservation
program to replace the A. A. A. To-
cused attention today upon Iowa stud
les pointing to the need for safeguards
to protect the Nations most valuable
natural resource-the soil.


Iowa State College land use spe-
cialists who conducted the studies
neither approved nor disapproved the
National Farm Committees proposed
A. A. A. substitute. They have, how
ever. during their approach to the
land use problem in the last five years,
advanced soil conservation as the
foundation stone of any sound pro-
gram.


Regarded Inseparable Link.


The college land planners found
that soil conservation was inextricably
linked with the problems of farm ten
ancy. farm debts, farm leases, the
cropping systems and the size and
type of farm.


Soil erosion was described as the
farmers public enemy No. l." Sur
veys showed that more than so per
cent of Iowa's land, among the most
productive in the Nation, had lost
about fourth of all its top soil by
erosion and that about a tenth of the
land under cultivation was virtually
worthless for tillage purposes.


1t was found that from a conser-
vation viewpoint Iowa farmers planted
per cent too many acres to corn;
harvested 4 per cent too much small
grain acreage, and lacked by per
cent enough hay and grass crops to
build up the soil.


Opinion of Specialists.


The specialists said:


Farm owners were better farmers
than tenant farmers. Tenant farm
ers, on the average, put greater per-
centage of their land into intertilled
crops, raised less pasture and en-
ployed cropping systems that did not
control erosion.


Tenant farmers operating under
long-term leases used cropping prac-
tices more conducive to soil conserva-
tion than did tenant farmers operat-
ing under short-term leases


Operators of large farms used more
desirable cropping methods than op-
orators of small farms.


Farmers heavily in debt tended to
~over crop" their farms, or work
their land too hard in order to get
out from under the debt burden.

7-HE waking dream became real


dream. and Tamara slept deep


and awakened in the delicious


l. dewy freshness of the Summer
morning with no time for further in
trospection. The whole house was astir

. stood at turn of the road-Tam in a

and lighter blues. with brimmed blue

looking browner than ever in white

Fifteen minutes later George and
Tamara kissed the others good-by and
climbed into the waiting car. With a
final wave from Tamara's hand they
went down the shady road and turned
into the highway The miles began to
slide by; the closely packed environs
of San Francisco were gone; they
struck out westward across the long
bridge that spanned the upper bay and
the marshes and caught the first hot
breath of the tremendous reaches of
the fruited valley beyond.


There was stop at the Lake Hotel
to freshen and change and to enjoy
with ravenous appetites the impromptu
meal of eggs and corn and fresh hot
rolls. Then Tam appeared once again
in the camping regalia of jeans and
sweater, red handkerchief and brim.
med hat, lineup and bowie knife, and
the late afternoon rocking chair sit
ters on the wide hotel veranda saw the
= tall. lean cowboy lead up the horses
and Tam and George mount them and
the little cavalcade set off for the tim
berline country.


The outfit" was composed of the
3 Iaconic Roy and his nephew, young
Roy. four horses and four pack mules.
In Roy's kyacks. strapped securely
with greasy, heavy belts to the mules,
was the entire camp equipment-a
dressing tent, the canvas bags and the
sleeping bags, the stove and pans and
groceries, the guns and fishing tackle.
The long shadows of the horses legs
and their own shadows lay before them
as they turned eastward, and the glory
of the late Summer afternoon pos
kessed a hushed and dreaming world.


Hits all of miles to camp; that
goin' to be too much for Mis- Davis?"
Roy had asked; Tam had said eagerly
that it would not be at all too far.
She loved riding and she loved Sally,
the big, gentle mare who was carry
ing her so high and so lightly. Wall.
! brung some stuff where kin break
1t out SOS you two kin camp down
anywheres if ye git too tired!' Roy
had said, expectorating. He had not
spoken again for the first magical
mile-a mile of silence and fragrance
and beauty along an old dirt road
that had once led the feet Of pioneers
into the gold mountains.


Presently he said abruptly: Guess
you'd better put her at that bank,
Mis- Davis!"


"Put?" Tam asked refining in, her
eyebrows raised. There was, to be
sure, an effect of the earth and the
roots on the steep bank at her right
having been scrambled over or dragged

Baboons either walk or run on all

heavy, overhanging eyebrows are very

Hunting for food, they climb swift
" over the trees to reach the fruit.

owner is approaching. Bulbous roots,
insects and reptiles are sought. Stones

feet are brown. his name dark red
dish brown, the hairs being ringed

color also. The grayish whiskers are
tipped with brown and grow back
ward, sideburn style. The tufted
tail is carried erect, the long tuft OF
hair falling toward the baboon's back.
Brown, cream, burnt umber colors
mingle with the brownish-gray body
colors. The callosities are large and
the flesh Is colored.


In spite Of their threatening atti-
tude and quick temper, 1t is not be-
leved that these balloons ever attack
man.

BY the Associated Press.


PARIS, July 1.-two red parades
swarmed through Paris today as
France celebrated the anniversary Of
the fall Of the Bastille in 1889.


The marchers we're celebrating not
only the revolution which overthrew
the monarchy, but also the victory OF
the Peoples Front" in the elections
six weeks ago.


Police and mobile guards, watchfrl
lest the celebrations develop into riots
with Nationalists, broke up series Of
petty clashes.


Mobile guards we're called for brief
actions In Barbecue and Lille.


In the capital the Peoples Front
professions converged on the Bastille
following great army parade through
the length of the city. The soldiers
were reviewed by President Lebrun
and. for the first time in history.
Socialist premier, Leon Blum.


Masses Of Red Flags Wave.


In the civilian professions masses Of
red flags. with the Communist hamme-
and sickle emblem in the center and
tricolor patches on one corner, waved
above the marchers heads.


Men. women and children swung
along together.


Truckloads of Communist children
joined with their elders in singing the
"Internationale" and shouting ''Soviets
everywhere!"


Red predominated in the costume,
many marchers wearing red hats, red
shirts and red skirts.


Many of the women had decorated
their dresses with three arrows, the
symbol Of the Peoples Front.


Communist cells (units) carried
banners with the names of the fac
tories in which their members work.


Over most of the routes of march
few policemen were to be seen. Their
main forces remained out of sight,
while 10000 carefully selected mem
bers of the Leftist party kept their
marching forces orderly.


Paraders Estimated at 100000.


The total number Of paraders was
unofficially estimated at more than
O.000.


As they passed a stand where
chorus of 800 voices sang revolutionary
songs, the marchers saluted huge pic
lures of the famous Leftists. Voltaire,
Rousseau and Jaures


They also saluted pictures of Rouget
de Lisle. composer of the "Marsail-
laisc, and of Eugene POTTER, composer
of the "Internationale.


Police estimated the crowds had
svelled to 100000 when Premier Blum,
accompanied by his wife and an off,
clal party, mounted the speakers
tribune in the Place de la Bastille.


Followers of the Peoples Front gov
ernment-including Socialists, Radi-
cal Socialists and Communists -
masSed into two huge marching COL
umns in the factory suburbs.


Thousands cheered the annual mill
tary parade which preceded the politi-
cal celebration and filled the area
around the Arch of Triumph with
martial display Of tanks and field
guns.


Shouting, pushing crowds thronged
the boulevard as the parade progressed.


"Hurray for Blum! Hurray for the
Peoples 'FRONT.'" shouted the Leftists.
"Hurray for the Army of France
for the French!" shouted back Ma
tionalists.


A few scufies occurred along the
route but mobile guards lining the
avenue shoulder to shoulder prevented
an outbreak of disorders.

The ancient Greeks. who invented

was your soul. 1t entered and lett

exhaling. During sleep 1t wandered

For several centuries, the breath
scientists were interested in locatlng
the exact spot where the soul re-
sided. The best they could make out
was that the heart was the true place
of contact between body and soul. This
was easy to infer. When one was
depressed, the soul was partially alb
sent. Peculiar bodily feelings in the

depression. In exalted moments the
opposite feelings seemed to center in
the region of the heart. More breath
(souD was present. Our own refer
ences to brave heart" and faint
heart" are traditions handed down
from the time that psychology was

An old Eskimo trick today helped

The drama and heartbreak of
tragic baby mixup" that rocked
Atlanta and twisted the lives Of
two families II years ago was
renewed today when an attrac-
tive young lady-who was the
baby in this strange tangle-an-
nounced she had become con-
vinced the courts had awarded
her to the wrong family.


While the city wondered at
the unusual turn of affairs, the
families of John Garner and
Daniel Pittman prepared to con-
fer over the future of the young
lady known for II years as
Louise Madeline Pittman, but
who now has decided she is Mary
Elizabeth Garner.


Two baby girls entered this
world at an Atlanta hospital in
1919. One was named Louise
Madeline Pittman and the other
Mary Elizabeth Garner. They
were born one day apart, and a
few days later Mrs. Pittman an
nounced that she had been given
the wrong baby-that the child
she had been given was in reality
the daughter Of Mrs. Garner.


Babies Exchanged


The babies were exchanged over
the protest of the Garner family,
who were convinced the baby
originally given to them was really
their own.


Steve johnson, who then was
superintendent of the hospital,
was a sort of umpire" in set
ting the tangle, deciding that
Louise Madeline should remain
with the PittmanS and Mary Eliza
beth with the Garners.


Only few months later,
though, tragedy struck again.
The girl known as Mary Elizabeth
Garner died of pneumonia. The
same day, Louise Madeline vas
severely burned. Mary Elizabeth,
whose parentage was still mys-
terry. was buried as Mary Elizabeth
Garner.


The Garners brought court pro-
ceedingS to gain custody of Louise
Madeline, but records show the
habeas corpus proceedings we're
dropped. The two families assert,
however, that the late Judge
George L. Bell ruled that the girl
would be permitted to make her
own choice when she reached the
age of accountability.
Then Years Pass


Years passed, and the Pittmans
moved to Florida. There neigh
Dor told Louise Madeline of her
uncertain parentage. Today she
said:


"Since that time 1 have felt


that I was not a Pittman."

LONDON, June 3 Q.N.SO.-The
central figure in Britain's "bitter
humiliation" over her defeat in
the eight months Geneva battle
with Italy, Emperor Halle SelasSie
Of Ethiopia, arrived today in the
land of his Staunchest supporter.
English cheers greeted him, but
there was no official reception.


Crowds lined the docks at South.
ampton as he disembarked from
the British liner Oxford. They ap-
plauded the hatless exile and the
train route to London found fire.
quent clusters of shouting town
and country people.


Waterloo Station, his terminus
in London, was filled early with
crowds, some persons waving the
Union Jack, while in Soho, the
Italian quarter, silence ruled.


Halle Selassie proceeded directly
70 the London house that had been
prepared for him. His diplomatic
aides sought an audience with
King Edward for him.


To avoid further friction with
Italy, and embarrassment" to
Britain, however, the Negus came
incognito, thus eliminating the
need for any official reception to
him as a monarch. Two special
men from Scotland Yard were as
signed to guard him.


The Negus arrived, cheered in
defeat, at the same time that
Marshal Pietro Badoglio, pro-
claimed viceroy of Ethiopia, was
being lonized upon his triumphant
return to Italy.

This is official cleanup week and
citizens are expected to round out
the drive for a cleaner Capital. which
the City Refuse Division inaugurated
last week with an intensive street and
alley cleaning campaign.


Householders are urged by tne Com
missioners to get rid Of all accumu-
lated rubbish and refuse; to wash,
paint and redecorate. The city gov
ernment will shift emphasis from
street cleaning to the collection serv-
ices and trash, ash and garbage col
lectors will be available to answer
special requests for carting away ma
terial piled up over considerable
period of time.


Data Is Advanced.


Cleanup week usually is set for
MAY, but the Commissioners advanced
the date in response to The Stars
campaign to make Washington look
its best for Spring visitors.


The Refuse Division completed its
week of extra activity last night, re-
porting that each of 598 miles of
paved streets had been cleaned at
least three times. Most streets were
washed by flushers. All were swept.


Evidences of the drive were appar-
ent to a reporter who visited yes
terday some of the sections where dirt
conditions were most acute before
the campaign started.


Public cooperation, given voluntar-
lily or stimulated by warnings that
police will take stern measures against
violators of anti-flth regulations,
seemed to have increased to a point
where it has facilitated greatly the
work of street and alley cleaners.


Alleys filled with refuse ankle deep
two weeks ago were more than rea-
sonably clean. Improper discard OF
trash and garbage had practically
ceased.


Thoroughness Apparent.


In some of the choice residential
areas, where householders had beer
littering alleys and street curbings
with lawn rakings and other debris
almost spotless conditions prevailed
The heaps of rubbish that were scat.
tered in alleys less than two weeks
ago had disappeared.


The Salvation Army announced yes.
terday that it would cooperate dur
ing cleanup week by sending truck,
or wagons to answer calls for rubbish
removal. The army is equipped with
10 trucks and six wagons. 1t was
pointed out that newspapers, maya
zines, rags, old clothes, etc. can be
used profitably, the organizations So
cial service center employing 90 needy
men to reconstruct such material fol
useful purposes.

For two years the United

Europe and North America. For

Germany have been flying the
South Atlantic. But Great
Britain has not been ready, and

the loot at Versailles saw to that.

evident that the planes which

ders to drop bombs could also fly

men.

Meanwhile, q newly-formed girls
regiment of militia started train

under arms failed to create a stir,
for brave women are far from ex-
ceptional in Spain from time i'm
memorial.


The regiment was formed in the

thousands of girls clamored to be

already are fighting.


The minister of war left Madrid

For the first time since the re-

most normal today. Men and
women of all classes strolled in

tected.


For once, almost no young men

By the Associated Press.


MADRID, March 13.-Spains riot
vexed officials, stepping IN to protect
British engineers against threats OF
violence to foreigners, today traced
assassins' arms they said were made
In Germany.


Authorities, it was understood, as
sured the British Embassy of protec-
ton for English engineers working on
the Zafra Railway in Huelva Province.
Extremists had threatened the en-
gineers with violence unless they fed
the country, picketing the zafra oftiees
and shouting Foreigners work in
Spain while Spanish engineers starveP


List Persons With Arms.


The director of public safety said
the police had obtained a list of per-
sons possessing arms such as were
used in yesterdays attempt to kill
Luis Jiminez Asua, Chamber of Depu-
ties leader and Socialist criminal at
torney.


The arms, they said, were manu-
factured in the Reich. Jiminez es-
capped unhurt, but his police body
guard was killed and seven Fascists
arrested.


While nuns and priests fled from
converts, the targets of repeated at
tacks in the rioting which has claimed
scores of lives since the February 10
elections, gendarmes arrested Com
munist for attempting to burn the
Salvador church in the heart OF
Madrid.


They said he was the same man ar
rested three years ago for bomolng
the Portuguese Embassy. The church.
on Anton Martin Square, was drenched
with gasoline and set ablaze, but fire.
men extinguished the flames.


New Clashes in Madrid.


Shots were fired by extremists and
police in Granada and Madrid wit
messed new Fascist-Leftist clashes.


There were rumors. unconfirmed or
denied, that several prominent Fascists
and Monarchists were marked Tor
death and that general strike is due
Monday, when Parliament reopens.


Fascists who tried to storm Premier
Manuel Azana's Office were beaten of.


The new Leftist government, despite
denials, was reported planning en-
ergetic measures to halt the disorders,
which the Socialist Executive Com
mittee declared were spurred "by
Rightists who are bitter over their
defeat in the general elections and are
seeking to discredit the Leftists."

The so-called "seventeen-year locusts"
are here again, in countless thousands,
probably millions in this vicinity. A
few days ago they began to emerge from
the ground, leaving innumerable holes
in the soil. Immediately upon reaching
the surface they started their slow crawl
toward the nearest trees or shrubs, up
which they climbed, seeking twig or
leaf beneath which they clung. Then
the back of the shell split open and the
winged cicada emerged, leaving the husk
behind. The male cicada lives only a
short time and takes no food. The female,
which lives for several weeks, deposits
her eggs about the middle of June. The
young hatch, drop to the ground and
burrow into the soil. there to subsist upon
the sap Of rootlets and to remain for
seventeen years. when the process is
repeated.


In the suburbs of washington these
cicada are Just now to be found in
immense numbers. They are commonly
called locusts, but that is not their
proper name. They do no particular
harm above ground. but in their long
burrowing they take the sustenance OF
growing things. While they are under
ground they take their toll from all the
vegetation.


Garden keepers are usually concerned
greatly when these little creatures come
into evidence, and seek to destroy them,
though that is huge task when the
swarms come forth as they are coming
at present. The birds take their toll Of
them, also. Even some Of the domestic
animals acquire Q taste for them and
help to keep down the brood that will
resppear in another seventeen-year
period.

The Sunday night of July 81, 1861,
found Richmond hot and terror
stricken, says the Richmond Times
Dispatch. The first big battle of the
war had been fought a few hours be-
fore, the first Battle of Manassas.
They were telling it around that the
Federal troops had won great VIC
tory and were marching on Rich
mond; and that there had been blood
shed past all belief.


During the night, dispatch from
Jefferson Davis, who was at the scene
of the battle, stopped half these
rumors: I'VE have won glorious
though bought victory. Night
closed on the enemy in full flight
and closely pursued"


Dearly Bought Victory.


How dearly bought this victory was,
Richmond saw "a hours later on that
stormy Monday night when the first
ambulance train arrived in a down.
pour Of rain. bearing the wounded.
The cry was for more stretchers, more
instruments, more torniquets, more
stimulants-more of everything that
would ease maddening pain, help am
putate splintered limbs and make
sound bodies once again out of that
sorry mess of blood and protruding
bones. 1t was not sight for those
who held that war was glorious.


Among the women who went down
to minister to the wounded was Miss
Sally Tompkins.


Women were thought to be retiring
creatures in the day of 81, but not
10 days after she had seen the first
of the hundreds of wounded men that
poured into Richmond from Manassas
Miss Sally had opened up a hospital
1t stood on the northwest corner of
Third and Main, the home of Judge
John Robertson, who had taken his
family to the country, and who. in
answer to Miss Sally's frantic pleas
for a hospital, had turned over to her
his dwelling.


Robertson Hospital.


With the little money she had Miss
Sally equipped her hospital, which she
called the Robertson Hospital. During
the four years of the war she nursed
1884 wounded men. There were no
trained nurses There were The Ladies
of the Robertson Hospital" women
who gave their services and offered
courage and willingness in place of
formal training. There were seven
surgeons, all of whom gave their serv-
ices, and stewards. And there was
gardener, a wounded man, who
raised fine vegetables in the back
yard of the hospital. and carpenter,
another wounded man, who made
chairs and other furniture. One OF
the chairs may be seen in the Con-
federate Museum.

BINGHAMTON, N. Y, March l8.--
Binghamton prepared today to face
flood conditions more severe than those
of last July, when 1000 families were
made homeless and hundreds OF thou
sands of dollars of property damage
resulted from high waters.


The Chenango and Susquehanna
Rivers, swollen by three days of heavy
rains and melted snow. pounded over
their banks, submerging highways,
rushing into houses and imperiling
the city's water supply.


The Susquehanna, already higher
than the 1885 flood crest, swept over
its bank near Court street and swept
toward the water works, where a sand
bag barricade served to keep back
flood waters for the, present.


Regarding the situation as every Sc
riouS," city engineers said that If water
reached the pumps, putting them out
of commission, there was but a days
supply stored in Mount Prospect Res
ervoir.


Families in the city's First Ward Sec
tion, worst sufferers of the 1885 food,
began moving their possessions from
their homes before daybreak as the
Chenango poured into the low-lying
residential area in the northwestern
section of the city.


Four of the city's seven bridges were
closed as water flooded the approaches
and splashed over the hoorings. The
remaining spans were expected to be
closed later today, city officials said


Similar flood conditions prevailed
in nearby towns and villages. Streets
were under water in Whitney Point,
Towanda, Pa; Norwich, Oneonta,
Lisle. Walton, Waverly, N. Y, and
Owego.

MARTINSBURG, w. Va, March
18.-While 24-hour rainfall that left
an official precipitation of 2.45 inches
over the Eastern Panhandle had
stopped this morning, flood conditions
continued to threaten as tributary
streams, all out Of bank, poured water
into the Potomac and Shenandoah
Rivers, which were expected to reach
their peaks today or tomorrow.


Much damage was already reported
to highway and low lying lands.
Railroad traffic and highway travel
were both broken. but beginning to get
back to normal this morning.

morning was reported within feet
Of the Highway Bridge level and traf-
fic was suspended. Travel over the
bridge across the Potomac at Shep-
herdstown was suspended last night.

ern Panhandle and South Branch

erty away with them.

Merry Christmas!


Those words echoed from every
lip today as Washington cele-
brated its gayest, happieSt, mer-
riest Christmas in many a year.


There was perfect weather for
the holiday, and thousands OF
youngsters were out playing with
the toys Santa left for them dur
ing the night.


It was a holiday for almost every
person in the District and all were
enjoying it to the utmost. The
poor and needy and the homeless
were not forgotten on this day,
with missions and charitable in
titutionS distributing bags Of food,
toys for children, warm clothing,
while for the homeless there were
special meals and gaily decorated
trees to cheer them up.


Busy Night Before


Yesterday afternoon was the
busiest washington has ever seen.
Government offices closed early,
and stores we're packed with
shoppers intent on getting gifts
at the last minute.


Later thousands of persons
packed Lafayette Square for the
lighting of the National Christmas
Tree. President Roosevelt spoke
at this ceremony, extending his
Christmas greetings to the nation,
and then threw a switch, turn
ing on hundreds of lights on the
great tree.


Groups of carolers went through
the streets last night, singing the
age-old Christmas anthems, while
in scores of churches, beautiful
and fragrant with their Christmas
decorations, special musical pro-
grams were offered.


Later there came the solemn
midnight mass in every Catholic
church in the city. Episcopal
churches held communion services,
while many Protestant churches
also held services at midnight to
commemorate the birth of the
Savior.


Churches Crowded


Every church was packed to
capacity for the services, and
again today when special services
were held. The Salvation Army,
Volunteers of America, Central
Union Mission and others also
held special service, and then had
meals and baskets for the needy,
with entertainment programs to
cheer them.


At the White House almost the
entire Roosevelt family was as
sembled, and there was much
merrymaking and exchange of
gifts. Yesterday Mrs. Roosevelt
presented gifts to all of the White
House staff, and then went out
to attend one of the alley Christ.
mas tree services.


In the various embassies and
legations of the Capital the diplo-
mats celebrated Christmas in the
manner of their home lands.

BY the Associated Press.


VATICAN CITY, December l9.-
Pope Plus, reported recovering from
partial paralysis Of his lower legs. to-
day Cancelled his usual Christmas eve
audience with the College Of Cardi-
mails and the Papal Court.


The 7s-year-old pontiff reluctantly
ordered invitations, issued yesterday,
recalled upon the advice Of his physi-
clans, prelates said.


Informed sources said the Pope was
impressed by the fact that every un-
usual exertion during the last few
days had been followed by a period Of
weakness.


Instead Of receiving the cardinals,
the pontiff will see them individually
during the next few days in his sick
room.


Again last night, doctors kept a
constant vigil over the Pope to quiet
his sleep when shortness Of breath
caused him to gasp and stir in his
bed.


Within. and outside the Vatican,
Catholich speculated over the Pom
tiff's successor when prelates in the
Holy See disclosed that Cardinal Pa
celli, papal secretary of state. had
taken over temporary direction of
ecclesiastical affairs.


The realization grew that Pope Plus
might never recover completely.


Passes Calm Night.


He passed a reasonably calm night,
gaining much more rest than the
night before, but reliable reports said
he had not slept soundly for several
nights.


His physicians were anxious that he
be kept from aggravating the con-
gested blood condition which forced
him to bed two weeks ago in great
pain from legs so swollen they were
partly paralyzed.


Since modern custom dictates that
new Pope be chosen from among the
cardinals, theoretically there are 66
possible heirs to the papacy. Actually,
however. there are few from whom the
selection would be made


Advance age, birth outside Italy and
diverse other barriers to the highest
Office in Roman Catholicism dim
whatever hopes most may have.


Three Names Listed.


Three princes OF the church are re-
garded now BY informed Vatican
sources as most likely successors:


Eugenio Pacelli, secretary Of state.


Ella Dalla Costa. Archbishop Of
Florence.


Luigi Lavitrano. Archbishop of
Palermo.


Although Pacelli is the most promi-
nent of the Cardinals by virtue of his
office. Vatican prelates said his name
might be overlooked when a new Pope
is chosen.


His tenure as nunzo in Germany
and his negotiation Of concordates
with Prussia, Bavaria and Germany,
it was said, might create opposition
among the seven French cardinals,
who might fear he had German lean
lngs.

Decentralization of flood devastated
San Angelo started yesterday as the
turbulent Concho River, subsiding
after the most destructive rise in its
history, left hundreds of destitute
refugees and property losses estimated
at $2,OOO,O0O.


Mud Uttered the streets and caked

SIDE was strewn with drowned sheep
and goats, communications were dis
rupted and public services were barely
functioning. But the city's 26, 900 in
habltants came through the disaster
without loss of life.


Cessation of heavy rains on wa
tersheds of the Concho's three branch
es apparently brought an end to the
nigh water which isolated San An
gelo, washed away more than 300
homes and damaged TOO others.


Business men raised a $500 emer-
gency fund for feeding and housing
the homeless hundreds. The rescue
OF six persons stranded in tree-tops
for "a hours near Plum Greek COM
munity relieved fears that the flood
would add death to its toll.


A horseman carried Mr.. and Mrs.
Eugene Weaver, their two children,
Robbie, 2, and James, 4, and two
marooned boatmen, Henry Boyd and
Robert Chanute, to safety. Eugene
Heshew, who rowed out yesterday
with Boyd and Chanute to rescue the
Weavers. reached safety earlier. The
Red Cross set up soup kitchens in two
churches. More than 300 destitute
persons were taken care of today.

SOMETIMES in Spring, but more


often in Summer or Autumn, the
migratory salmon in the sea prepare
for their long, hungry Journeys up
stream for the purpose Of laying their
eggs.


The trips are difficult and long and
lean, for the hsh are often obliged
to Jump up over waterfalls and other
such obstacles, and they travel hum
dreds of miles without eating on the
way. And whenever they come to q
fork they choose the colder branch
10 travel along.


It is a very serious and arduous
undertaking, not only because of the
perils of the trip and the discomfort
of the starvation diet, but because
the egg-laying venture itself Is very
thorough and extensive among salmon.


First, the female scoops q fiat place
in the gravel near some cool spring,
II she can find ont, for spring water
freezes less easily than river water.
Then, between October and January.
the female lays her eggs-about 900
Of them for every pound of her weight.


After the spawning the salmon often
die. II they are lucky, they drift
back to sea. where they can feed
once more on herring and mackerel
and the other fish upon which they
thrive.


The young salmon hatch In from

THERE is something grandiose


and awe-inspiring in natural


catastrophies. They re-estab-


L lish a sense of proportion
They remind man. the only paranoiac
amongst the an..lals. that he lives
dangerously and is not yet lord over
all of nature. At the same time. and
for brief moments. they release the
heroism and the sacriflcial spirit Of
wars. without the hatred and bad
conscience with which war cankers
the soul.


They wipe out. for moment, class
lines and race lines; they shift owner
ship of property: they raze rich mems
houses and slurs, and all without
creating the antagonisms of economic
warfare. The banker on the roof
top, wigwagging for a rescuer. asks
nothing better than to be in the same
boat-any old boat-with the relief
worker When the Mississippi rose
few years ago, and broke the levees.
Red Necks" who in more fortunate
times enjoyed the fiesta of lynchings,
swan out to rescue stranded black
men. Water. fire. earthqu2ke-these
things do not divide men. They bring
them together.


Brings OUT Noble Qualities.


In such natural catastrophies men,
for the most part. show their noblest
and most decent human qualities.
There are. of course, exceptions. In
Hartford the police had to take sharp
measures against looters. But for
every one who uses catastrophe for
his own gain, there are a hundred
who show exceptional courage. endur-
ance and generosity. Men also dis
play their genius. No modern civili-
zation has been permanently wrecked
by forces of nature. The streams
swell into torrents, the torrents rush
into oceans. the great waves of water
rise and break the confines built
against them: they descend greasily
inexorably upon fields. factories and
cities. Crops are drowned, factory
chimneys topple into the tide, mort
cages - are wiped out. Epidemics
flourish.


But when the flood subsidies and
the water recedes physicians mobilize
against the plaques; farmers go out
again with plows and hoes; brick
layers and carpenters rebuild broken
walls: new homes rise on the wrecks
of old ones. Neither Nation nor city
perishes.


Indeed. the catastrophe Is too soon
forgotten. Were mems memories longer
they would prepare against, its re-
currence. 1t is scandalous that in
this country Of builders and engineers
we have not controlled flood water
The reason is not lack of knowledge or
power. 1t is only the perversity Of
human nature. For no gigantic pub
lie works such as these can be under
taken without stepping on some
body's toes.


The same difficulty attends slum
clearance. Everywhere some special
interest has to be sacrificed for the
general good. Billions have been
spent in the last two years, but not
on the great works vitally needed.
Why not? For two reasons: Such
works take long-range planning. This
country greatly needs a permanent
body Of engineers. as divorced from
politics as is the War College, insured
in their positions by long appointments

into Hendaye tonight to cut Of fleeing
Socialist government troops and con-

The Fascists drove of desperate
government fighters who sought to
retain the Spanish end of the bridge
into France after fleeing the rebel fire
that marked the fall of Irun.


Four armored cars, camouf1aged
with tree branches, rumbled through
the ruined city and bore down on
the fleeing Irun defenders, who sought
refuge in a few isolated trenches and
fields.

was unknown. There were reports 100

on charges of political padding in the
Democratic campaign.

unquestioned employees would receive
their April salaries by Monday at the
latest.

Chicago ruled that Stelle should not
hold up the pay Of employees not in
volved In the padding charges.

Gov. Homer had padded the Code De-
partment pay roll with the names Of
5000 campaign workers.


In the controversy. the Governors
spokesmen retaliated that Stelle and
Auditor Edward j. Barrett, affiliated
with the Kelly Nash Democratic organ
ization which opposes the faction led
by Gov. Horner, seeking renomina-
tion, had padded their own pay rolls.

By the Associated Press.


VATICAN CITY, December 2s.-Dr.
Amanti Milani. chief physician to
Pope Plus XII. made thorough check
of the holy fathers condition today
after a night Of what attendants de-
scribed as excruciating pain.


DR.. Milani kept close watch on the
Pope throughout the restless night.
visiting the sick room several times
after reliable reports said the partial
paralysis had spread from the legs
along the left side and arm.


Despite his condition, the Pope dis
cussed ecclesiastical problems with
Pietro Cardinal Fumasoni, former
papal delegate to Washington and
now head of the Vatican department
for propagation of faith.


Leg Painful and Swollen.


Two doctors and a hospital attend
ant were constantly at the holy
fathers side. Dr. Milani spends about
five hours daily with the Pope. The
left leg was said to be particularly
painful yesterday and was swollen to
a marked degree.


At morning masses, prayers for the
alienation of the pain suffered by his
holiness mingled with the usual de-
vout pleadings that his life be con-
tinued.


Even during the spasms Of suffer-
ing, reports said, the aged pontiff
showed stanch good cheer and be-
tween the intervals of pain drifted
into sound sleep.


The fact the 79-year- r-old Pope was
able to take only slight nourishment
added to his extreme weakness.


Prelates Show Strain.


Most Vatican prelates, observing
tradition, resolutely attempted an off,
cial air of optimism, but the strain
was obvious.


Attendants moved with softened
tread. All Vatican affairs were con-
Quoted In an atmosphere so hushed
it seemed all of the little city was q
sick room.


The holy father heard morning
mass from the chapel adjoining his
bed room after DR.. Milani finished
his examination.


Vatican prelates disclosed that the
Pope himself vetoed the issues Of
periodical bulletins on his condition.


They said he described his illness
as painful and perhaps lengthy, but
nothing to worry about.

TIENTSIN, May 30.-Two acts of
violence further embittered Sino-Japa-
nese relations today. The first was
the destruction of bridge at Chuan-
liangchen. between Tangku and Tient-
sin, and the second was an alleged
attempt to wreck a Japanese troop
train.


Chinese authorities said they feared
the japanese might construe the sab
otage as an answer to Japan's action
In sending more troops to North
China garrisons.


The incidents occurred without cas-
uaities, but Japanese military authori-
ties took grave view of the situation.
Intelligent Chinese sources deplored
the episodes, declaring Japan might
welcome such occurrences as pretext
for armed Intervention In North China.


Extreme nervousness prevailed in
Tientsin, where there is a considerable
American colony and where 800 Amer
ican soldiers are quartered.


The two incidents arose last night
Just after Japan, overriding Chinese
protests, landed 5000 fresh troops for
its North China garrisons, bringing its
military strength here to nearly 10000
men.


Bridge Is Dynamited.


Apparently seeking to block trains
bearing the newly arrived japanese re-
Inducements into the interior, un-
known persons blew up the Chuan-
liangchen Bridge on the Peiping-
Liaoning Railroad between Tientsin
and Tangku, eastern port, where the
troops were landed.


Train service between Tientsin and
Shanhaikwan, at the eastern end of
China's great wall, was suspended, and
one train, loaded with japanese troops.
failed to arrive here from Tangku.


Complicating the already serious
situation. another japanese military
train bringing infantry reinforcements
to Tientsin narrowly escaped destruc-
ton when a charge of explosives was
set of under the rails over which
the cars were running.


Only a number of japanese Army
horses were injured.


The train moved on under its own
steam to the Tientsin Railway station,
where japanese military authorities
instituted an investigation imme-
diately. They said the explosives were
wired elaborately to be set off auto
matically as the train passed over
them.


Both incidents occurred in the path
of the troops moving into Tientsin,
destination of the majority of the
fresh forces. Informed sources as
sumed the explosions were intended
as an attempt to Illustrate Japan's
military plans in North China.


Tension Is Tightened.


The two new North China ex-
plosions contributed to growing
array of incidents, charges and
counter charges tightening Sino-
Japanese tension.


The Chinese have protested against
Japan's reinforcement Of its northern
garrisons as unwarranted, have
charged Toxic with supporting North
China smuggling and have accused
the Japanese military Of encroaching
on North China provinces.


The Japanese have replied that
increased military power was neces-
sary to protect their interests in
North China.

Both the Swiss and the Dutch, who,

powers abandoned it, conceded that
Frances action makes continued adher-
ence untenable. The Berne and Hague
governments are proceeding forthwith
with devaluation measures essentially
like those for which Premier Blum is
seeking parliamentary authority in
Paris today. Thus Italy, Germany and
Poland remain the only important
European states which have not been
impelled to resort to drastic currency
reform in consequence of the epochal
nglo-Franco- American agreement and
what led up to it. The Italians await
the immediate results of the pact, amid
widespread expectation at Rome that
Ira devaluation is inevitable. The Ger
mans, too, are adopting watchful
attitude. 1t seems improbable that the
Reich, with devaluation on all sides,
can long resist adjusting the mark to
the franc and the pound. The Poles
insist that the position of the zloty for
the present renders devaluation unneces-
sary, although Warsaw proclaims fealty
to the stabilization accord in principle.


While the gold standard was giving
up the ghost in most of those quarters
1t has been fighting a precarious battle
for it's life. Washington was the scene OF
q dramatic exhibition of the potency OF
the stabilization alliance. Word having
been flashed from Wall Street that the
Soviet State Bank had dumped million
pounds of its sterling on the New York
market for sale at the best price obtain
able, Secretary Morgenthau instantly
drew upon his $4,000, 100000 stabilization
fund to the extent of $5,000,000 and
bought Russias pounds. accompanied by
announcement that there was more
where that came from. Whether the
Moscow maneuver was deliberate effort
to depress sterling or routine operation
to stave off anticipated loss from fall
in exchange, it gave the United States
a welcome opportunity to demonstrate
the defensive power of the monetary
entente. The drop in pound value was
Immediately checked. Uncle Sam turned
a tidy penny in profit, and all con-
cerned were put on notice that they will
monkey at their peril with the triple
toothed stabilization buzz-saw.

When homeward from his busy day the
toiler travels far
He'll simply push a button when he
wants to stop the car;
The man will pull lever and the door
will open wide
And gently jolt him down the step into
the street outside.
A button he will press to start the ele.
vator,s flight;
Another button floods the room with
soft electric light.
And then to cheer the WEAKNESS that
comes at close of day
He throws a switch and turns a knob
and lets the music play.
Oh, what's the good of hands and feet
and what's the good of brain
When with such little effort men such
ample service gain?
What call is there to strive and wait
and theorize and guess,
When all you need is to decide which
button you will press?

THE effects of last Springs fooA


and this Summers drought have
been such that one of the finest trout
streams in New York State is Just
about ruined.


The high water during the floods
swept large numbers of the fish down
out Of the Willewemoc into the Bea-
verkill, another noted trout stream.
and on into the Susquehanna River.


Then when the high water subsidized
and conditions began to return to nor
NAL, the drought came along and
dried up many Of the little feeder
streams which normally swell the
Willewemoc into a stream often 80
feet wide.


The deep pools now are mere shall
low holes through which one can
wade, and many of the rapids have
been reduced to rock piles through
which a stream which would disgrace
a garden hose trickles.


The result is that this stream, which
annually lures thousands of fv fish
ermen from all over lower New York,
will be of little use for fishermen for
several years to come.

NOME, Alaska, August 15.-TWo
famous Russian flyers, charting pos
sible new airplane trade route, learned
first hand today about Bering Strait
fogs that sometimes rise $4,000 feet
and send airmen to their deaths


Taking off in fair weather near
Nome to cross the strait to Siberia, the
Soviet pilots, Sigismind Levanevsky
and Victor Levchenko, plunged into
binding fog over the water and sent
their pontoon-equipped monoplane
back-tracking to Alaska yesterday.
They landed at Teller, 60 miles north
Of here.


Levanevsky and Levchenko waited
for the fog to clear before resuming
their trip to their next objective,
Uelen.


1t was the third interruption by
weather the Russians encountered
since starting a 10,000-mile fight
from San Pedro, Calf, to Moscow
in quest of scientific data about
flying conditions in the high north.

Helen Keller is alone today. Her
teacher Is gone beyond the summons Of
her cropping fingers. Anne Sullivan Macy,
exhausted from the labors of career
dedicated to her fellow creatures, has
been released to her reward. But the
woman whose soul she freed from dark
ness and silence-a living tomb-denies
that she is lost. Rather, it is only her
pain, her suffering, that has terminated.
The immortality she earned by her self
less devotion to others will protect her
forever from the finality which men call
death.


Mrs. Macy was one of the most re-
markable characters of modern times.
The noble courage Of her mind and the
generous charity Of her heart won for
her the respect and the affection Of all
who knew her story. Her marvellous gifts
of intelligence and sympathy, her gentle
ness. her sraciousness and her humility
made her . benediction to Thousands.

TRENTON, N. j.. April 3.-Stunned
by the news that no further request
for a stay in Bruno Richard Haupt-
mann's execution would be made by
the grand jury, the condemned mans
wife, Anna, hoped frantically today
for another reprieve from Gov. Har-
old G. Hoffman.


Despite Gov. Hoffman's announce
ment less than a week ago. there will
be no second reprieve," Mrs. Haupt-
mann wanted to plead with him for
her husbands life.


Hauptmann's wife burst into tears
when she was informed of the Mercer
County grand jury's failure to indict
Paul H. Wendell on charge of Staying
the Lindbergh baby.


She wept again when she heard that
from the grand jury would come no
further request to prolong Haupt-
mann's life.


Confident After Last Visit"


Belief that the grand jury would
indict Wendell had been Mrs. Haupt-
mann;s strongest hope for her hus-
bands salvation.


MY husband will not die in the
electric chair. will see him again"
she said confidently yesterday after
her last visit" to Hauptmann per-
mitted under prison rules.
A thrice-repeated situation con-
fronted Mrs. Hauptmann today-the
task of watching the clock hands move
around toward his death hour.


She was awakened at her hotel,
ironically, by the gay strain, Happy
days are here again-and the skies
above are blue again." Justify sung
by an early riser who did not know
she was across the hall.


Made Trip to See Son.


The news from the grand jury ses-
sion that dashed her hopes reached
her after midnight, when she returned
from a hurried trip to New York to
see her 3-year-old son. Manfred.


She had left confident Hauptmann
would escape the chair and told the
child his father would be home soon.


Mrs. Hauptmanns decision to visit
her son, who is under the care of
friend in the Bronx, was made sud-
denly, after seeing Hauptmann at his
death cell for the last time permitted
under prison rules unless another
last st-minute delay comes.
She left without informing c. Lloyd
Fisher, Hauptmann's attorney, who
expressed surprise at her departure
when he called her room in vain for
a conference early last night.
Fled Tension of Trenton.


A wish to get away from the ten
sion of Trenton was given as the
main reason for her flight.
Hauptmann's son, as the execution
hour again approached, was under the
care of Miss Ruth Werner, daughter
of the Rev. D. G. Werner, who was
praying with Bruno Tuesday when
a last-minute delay saved the con-
demned man from death.
Manfred has not seen his father
for a year. On his last visit he was
carried into the Flemington jail.

SPERRYVILLE, Va, october 23.-
Rappahannock County has its first
chestnut crop in Is years. 1t isn't
large. but the nuts are of the finest
quality.


About nine years ago the late John
A. Browning of Greenfield, much dis
stressed over the loss Of all the
chestnut trees Of the county by blight,
set out so blight proof trees of the
Chinese and japanese varieties. Since
his death, which occurred shortly
after setting out the trees, his widow,
Mrs. Browning, with the assistance of
the United States Department OF
Agriculture, has cared for them. The
department will receive the first crop
for experimental purposes.


The trees have grown well and no
sign of blight has appeared. They
were pruned for the FIRST time two
years ago and were much improved
by the operation.

NEW YORK, April 4.-Commodity
prices declined during the past six
days. extending the current slump in
the staple markets to seven weeks, dur
ing which time the Associated Press
weighted wholesale index dropped 60
per cent.


The close of the combined index on
Friday was 1886, new low for the
year. and compares with 7416 last
week and 7432 year ago, with 1926
as 100.


From the beginning of 1926 to date,
the index has fallen So per cent.
Among its components, only non-fer-
rous metals and industrial staples are
above the starting levels. other groups
showing wide losses-food, IL per cent;
live stock. 7 per cent: agriculture, 10
per cent; textiles, II per cent.


Farm Group Down.


Leading the downturn this week is
the agricultural group again, with
wheat contributing largely to its reac-
ton. Grain traders continue to feel
that the domestic crop of both Spring
and Winter wheat will be above con-
sumptive needs.


Corn, oats and cotton dipped slightly.
while rye managed to chalk up small
gain. These farm products, for the
most part, continue under the same
cloud of uncertainty regarding both
the moisture possibilities and the ef-
fectivenesS of the administration sub
stitute for the defunct A. A. A. that
has been present for some time.


Mixed live stock prices resulted from
a sizable setback for cattle, a small
betterment in hogs and an unchanged
lamb quotation. Specialists in the
animals hold that prices should con-
tinue loWer-that large shipments of
hogs in the early Summer will out
weigh the effect of continued small
receipts Of cattle and lambs.


Food prices we're irregular, with the
more heavily weighted flour, lard and
butter depressing the index, despite
advances in eggs, sugar and cocoa.


Textile quotations have been yielding
to the pressure of expanding inven-
tories during the past few months
This week wool, cotton cloth and silk
dropped.


Swing to Rayon Seen.


The high level of silk prices has
made it cheaper for goods manufac-
turers to use rayon. The swing to
rayon in women's wear this Spring is
held to indicate that either the price
of silk or its use will come down.


Commodities going directly into in
dustrial channels moved against the
trend. Tin resumed its slow rise.
Bituminous coal and lumber were
buoyant, while rubber fell back frac-
tionally.

prise will absorb the bulk of the

est era of prosperity it has ever

Real and final recovery will
begin a week from tomorrow
when the people throw off the
weight of Federal interference

they elect Alfred M. LandOn."

Two civilian employees were injured
seriously when an explosion rocked
the two-story brick mine-testing lab.
oratory at the Navy Yard early this
afternoon.


Fire trucks rushed to the scene
and spent nearly an hour extinguish-
ing the blaze, removing high explosives
and spraying the first floor with chemi-
Gals.


The injured we're:


Joseph Ross. civilian ordnance man
reported severely hurt.


r. L. Watkins, civilian instrument
maker, overcome by smoke. He was
taken to public health hospital in old
Post Ofice Building at Twelfth street
and Pennsylvania avenue for treat
ment.


Building Full Of Explosives.


The building was full of high ex-
plosives and chemicals.


The first-door experimental lab
oratory was wrecked. Several win
dows were shattered by the detonation
The inside walls and window castings
were charred.


The laboratory is used for the test
ing of all mine ingredients, explosives
and powder.


More than six fire trucks, including
chemical apparatus, rushed to the
scene.


Cause of the explosion was not de-
termined Immediately.

commodity prices this week.

also came under the influence Of pos

cluding corn, oats and rye.

Of IS important wholesale commodities
dropped to 81 per cent Of the 1925
average from 81.47 last week, and
compares with 1881 year ago.

sharpest run-up since 1888, with for
ward orders covering requirements well
into 1887 being placed by many large
consumers. The sudden realization by
the trade that sustained retail demand
had reduced stocks to the lowest level
in years brought flood Of buying into
the market

nudged up also as prospects of the

lower.

high ground for the year in each Of
the past eight weeks. Steel bulets

heavy items have pushed ahead more
Bituminous coal, tin and

and burlap slipped back fractionally.

MOSCOW, October Is R.-Dic-
tator Joseph Stains remarkable dec
laration to Spanish Communists that
soviets are rendering every assistance
in their power" to Madrid stirred
widespread speculation today.


The Russian words used in Stalin's
telegram to the Central Committee Of
the Communist party in Spain left

every assistance" physically or within
the legal bounds of the international
non Intervention accord.


There was no official Interpretation.
In any event. however, informed
sources believed Stalin's message was
the most important indication that
the Soviets are prepared for early
action to change the present situation.

Returning from Vancouver, these
young soldiers-veteran plainsmen
now-became the guardian angels OF
all travellers, caravans and ranchers
against marauding Comanches and
Lapins during their reign of terror"
in Texas and kansas. There was
little open warfare, but incessant
hard riding and occasional punitive
forays when savages grew too bold.
How closely did the sharing Of peril
and loneliness unite this isolated band
Of men! They were blood brothers,
indeed. and their records, still intact,
depict the grief which every casualty
brought to the regiment.


Busy with the pioneering work OF
the West, the Mounted Rifiemen were
far removed from the questions trou-
bling North and South. It was q
sad moment when the guns Of Fort
Sumter tolled the war between the
States. With hearts full Of wretched-
ness, the regiment bade good-by to
the 10 officers, including their colonel.
who doffed blue uniforms for Con-
fede1ate gray. No enlisted man left
the regiment.

rising Of February 26.


The division, recruited from Toxic
and the surrounding prefectures, will
replace a division already en- route
home, and its departure therefore
does not mean the Japaneses forces
in the Japanese-sponsored Asiatic
state will be increased.


The divisions members recently
marched to Toxic shrines, taking the
vow to wipe out the smudge on their
record for joining the abortive rebel
lion early this year.

juring several persons and caus-

coast as San Francisco shook ur-
der its worst storm in IL years.

confined to their homes as the
storm brought an epidemic Of
colds or mild influenza and Off
cialS ordered schools in many out
lying cities closed.

versities of Stanford and Cali
fornia, and San Quentin prison,
where $50 convicts were reported
stricken.

day had one unidentified yacht
flashing distress signals, heavy
SHOWS blanketed the mountain re-
gionS, tying up automobile traffic.

ed by Mary AStor and Melvyn
Douglas, shooting mountain
scenes, was snowbound at Truckee,
Calf.

rotary plows were called In an
effort to clear roads and tracks.

fic was delayed and In some
points halted altogether in South
ern California.


In a score Of suburban towns
near Los Angeles, walls of water
roared down canyons onto resi-
dental sections, battling efforts
Of hundreds of flood control
workers. In some sections water
several feet deep was running
through streets.


More rain and continued storm
conditions were forecast by
weathermen.

Although the English setter is
one of the perennially popular
breeds of dog in the United States,
little is known of the origin and
characteristics of the breed.


Settlers are of several types, and
derive their names from the ken
nels of their original English
breeders. There is the Gordon
setter. developed from the kennels
Of the Dukes Of Gordon in north.
ern England. Belton and Llew.
ellyn settlers were named for their
original breeders.


Many SportSmen prefer the
Irish setter, a distinct type, diff
fering from his English cousin in
several respects. Irish settlers are
fast. enduring and have delicate
noses. They have beautiful red
coats. English settlers are usually
white, with flecks of black and
tan.


Settlers today are more deli.
cately formed than their heavier
ancestors. They are like pointers,
except that they have not the
pointers arched leg and back,
and as game dogs they are much
more careful workers in the field.


Gentle and companionable as
they are, the nature of settlers
often works against them.


Owners should never allow set
ters to grow fat and lazy. They
must be kept active to be at their
best.
