Feb. 17.-Norway held the Olym.
pic title, the flame on the tower
high above the ski stadium had
flickered out and athletes from all
over the world were en- route home
today following the closing of the
fourth winter Olympic games here
with a ceremony Of notable pag-
eantry, which was topped by q
stampede.


Chancellor Adolf Hitler and
most of his cabinet were present
on the final day of the competi-
ton to see Canada defeat the
United States at hockey, FL, to
give Great Britain the hockey
championship. Canada came Sec
ond in this department and the
United States third.


In the ski jump, Birger Ruud,
Of Norway, took first place, Sven
Ericsson, Of Sweden, second and
ALI Andersen, of Norway, third.


Hitler Satisfied


Hitler and his lieutenants were
obviously well satisfied with the
success of the ames, which
Avery Brundage, on behalf of
the United States, termed the
greatest ever held" At least
10000 persons paid admissions
to see the final ski jump event
and the closing ceremonies. Ger.
man officials said more than
SOC, 900 persons paid admissions
during the II days of the games.


In the closing ceremony in the
ski stadium, the gold, silver and
bronze medals were distributed
among the winning and placing
athletes. While each recipient
stepped forward, the band blazed
away at the national anthem of
his country, and army guns
doomed over the mountain tops.


Then thousands of torchlights
formed a giant horseshoe around
the ski jump and the president
of the International Olympic
Committee, thanking Hitler, the
German government and the
town of Garmisch-P Partenkirchen
for acting as hosts, formally de-
clared the games ended.


To the sound of trumpets and
the thunder of cannon, the
Olympic flag was hauled down
and the Olympic flame was
slowly extinguished.


AS the athletes marched out
the entire mountainside suddenly
blazed with fireworks.


Two Persons Injured


When all was over, Nazis kept
the huge crowd inside the ski
stadium for about two hours until
Chancellor Hitler and other off
cialS were able to depart. Two
persons were injured and others
tainted as the crowd battled and
milled about in an attempt to
leave the stadium or catch a
glimpse of the German chancellor.


Members of the Nazi labor serv.
ice corps, forming a solid Gordon
against the crowd, refused to let
anyone out until after Hitler had
departed.


Throughout the Gay Hitler was
in a jovial mood. During the
final ski jump contest, when the
crowd stated to cheer him, he
pointed laughingly at the ski
jump and motioned the crowd
to watch the skiers rather than
himself. He laughed and joked
continually.


Again, during the United States
Canada hockey game he chuckled
frequently, obviously enjoying the
bruising play Of both teams.

ever-menacing volcano Santa Rita.

possible any accurate estimate Of the

Crisis and chaos in Spain, more or less
chronic ever since King Alfonso was de-
throned five years ago this month, have
led to another kaleidoscope change in the
republics tangled political affairs. Presi-
dent Aicala Zamora, who was chiefly
responsible for the overthrow of the
monarchy in 1881, has been summarily
expelled from ofice. The custer was the
result of an overwhelmingly adverse vote
in the Cortes, which by 238 to decided
tionally dissolved parliament last Janu-
ary. The technical point on which the
CorteS based its action was that the
President had already exhausted his legal
right to prorogue parliament twice. The
motion declaring transgression of his
authority provided automatically for the
executives dismissal, in the midst of
term that still had year and eight
months to run. The presiding officer of
the Cortes, Senior Martinez Barrio, was
promptly installed as interim president
and will serve until there is another elec-
ton, in June.


The zamora administration always led
a precarious existence. From its outset
1t came under fire not only from the
Rightist- -Monarchist groups, which were
the presidents traditional opponents, but
from the Left Republicans, the Union
Republicans, the Socialists, the Com
munists and other factions, which among
them comprised the so-called Popular
Front" In consequence, Zamora's regime
was continuous chapter of fiercely par
tisan feuds and hatreds aggravated by
the Vaccinations of Alfonsos supporters
yearning for restoration of the monarchy,
by the rayages of depression and by the
ancient differences between church and
state. Opposition violence, destined to
end Ia Zamora's fall, became intensified
after the Leftist triumph In the February

aster. Starving and nearly frozen, they
finally were located by pilots flying Army
Air Corps planes and taken of by mem
bers of the crew of the Coast Guard
cutter Harriet Lane. One lad suffered
frost-bitten hands and feet, but his
comrades came through the ordeal un-
hurt-food and warmth restored them

be las good as new"

tragic. Indeed, it was mere accident
that the ice noe did not change position
sufficiently to precipitate the boys into
a compartment in Davy Jones locker.

PARIS, November 30. - Fury over
the suicide OF Roger Salengro, min
lister Of the interior, was intensified
today as anarchists slapped lurid
posters throughout the city advocating
an armed struggle If necessary
against tascism.


The government was alarmed that
resentment of Leftists, who charged
that Rightist accusations against the
minister led Salengro to take his own
life Tuesday night, might lead to Sc
we're violence.


Heavy reinforcements Of mobile
guards were ordered into the city
from the provinces.


Officials we're particularly anxious
about preserving order Sunday. A
huge Communist-called street protest
against "fascism-the assassin which
killed Salengro" was to be staged then
to coincide with the minister's funeral
at Lille.


Vast Demonstration Expected.


Authorities anticipated vast dem
onstration in the Place de la Repub-
lique and the Place de la Nation Sum-
day afternoon after other factions in
the popular front joined the Com
munist plans.


Premier Blum, Defense Minister
Edouard Daladier and Maurice Thorez,
secretary-general of the French Com
munist party, planned to speak at
another mass meeting tomorrow night.


The entire cabinet. 200 deputies and
100 senators planned to attend Salem
gro's funeral, as well as thousands of
Paris Leftists, for whom there were to
duced fares


The premier'S newspaper. lie Popu-
laire, indicated the government would
reject Communist demands for the
imprisonment of prominent Rightists
whose press campaigns against Salem
gro they blamed for the minister's
death.


(Salengro left a note saying he was
killing himself because of repeated
articles accusing him as war de-
serter. A military court acquitted him
of such charges)


The Communist political bureau had
demanded the arrest of former Premier
Andre Tardieu and two other Rightists,
Horace Carbuccia. editor of the Right
| ist weekly Gringoire, and Jean
Chiappe, former Paris police chief,


The government, meanwhile, sought
enactment of stringent laws against
defamatory press attacks. Blum will
present bill to the Chamber of Dep
uties November "a, which, modelled
after English law, should subject
editors and others responsible for
newspaper articles to criminal prose-
| cution for defamation.


A new wave of strikes added to the
governments difficulties. They were
based on union disputes. however. and
were not connected with Salengro's
death.

THE typical Sheraton sideboard has
either slender, turned and reeded
legs supporting a superstructure in
which there are deep drawers or cup
boards at either end and a shallow
drawer or cupboard in the middle Of
the shaped or straight front, or else
the ends are square, projecting some-
what from the straight middle portion,
and are carried down almost to the
floor as cupboards. These square
ends are oftentimes built up above the
top of the middle portion to serve az
bases for the support Of knife boxes or
urnS.


Sheraton also designed other side
boards OF a pattern which we often
associate with the name Of Hepple-
white. These sideboards had shaped
fronts and square tapered legs or round
tapered reeded legs and ends contain
ing drawers, and the middle portion
one shallow drawer, the part under
the drawer being left followed out for
the accommodation of a cellarette or
wine cooler. SideboardS Of this type,
however, can be ascribed TO designer
only approximately. They were gen.
orally made to order.


1t is known that Sheraton did not
favor the serpentine front, but pre-.
ferred square ends and sprung fronts,
or with the whole frcnt convex in
form. Knife boxes had either slant
tops or were made in the shape Of
urns. The square ended sideboards
with the eXtremitieS surmounted for
the knife urns took the place Of the
earlier sideboard tables, which, during
the Chippendale period, were elaborate,
rectangular oblong side tables sup
ported on four, sometimes six legs.


~ ***


&IDEBOARDS provided a medium


for display of inlay and veneer.
Feather edging, feather pattern OF
veneer or marqueterie banding and
block inlay was very popular. Fan
shape patterns and other motifs we're
used in corners. Handsome mounts
were very prominent. The mounts Of
Sheraton furniture were very similar
to that Of Hepplewhites. Both types
have engraved ovals with ring handles,
the round ringed or chased mounts
with either brass knobs or rings. ard
the octagonal mounts with ring ham
dies. The mounts used during the lat
/ ter part Of the Sheraton period often
has lion-headed handles with rings
pended from their mouths. The key
plates are generally diamond-shaped
ivory, flush with the surface Of the
door or drawer When ivory was not
used narrow, brass flush rim took its
place.


The later pieces often had ornate
| mother-of-pearl inlay, as well as
marqueterie banding. The sideboard
portrayed on this page was Of this
type. The owner, preferring to have
the more conservative veneer and in
lay only, had the pearl removed from
the cupboard door panels, replacing it
with the bell flower drop inlay. A
local cabinemaker achieved the trans.
formation.

Mrs. Hughes told police she did not

1t had been caused by the wind.

for work this morning. He noticed
the kitchen clock was missing, then
found burned matches scattered over
the floors. Further investigation re-
yealed the entire house, with the ex-
ception of the two bed rooms, had
been ransacked, although several val
liable silver pieces were overlooked.

notified police.

who entered two apartments at BIS

Atwood kept money. yielded several
flngerprints by which it may be pos
sible to establish the identity of the
thief, police said. About $50 in cash

ued at more than 5000 also were
missing.

Defeats at the polls, retirements and

CLEVELAND, Sept. IL. -Wash-
ington was in third place in the
American League today after a
stirring 7-to-2 victory yesterday
over the Cleveland Indians here.


The team that manager Bucky
Harris made no spring prognosti-
cation for other than to say that
it would keep fighting was higher
than it's most optimistic sup
porters had hoped it would be.


Behind the six-hit pitching of
the veteran Earl Whitehill, the
Senators had no difficulty beating
the highly touted Indians, five
runs in the first inning off Dennis
Galehouse settling the issue be-
yond all dispute.


Manager Harris must have
cleaned some personal satisfaction
out of the victory because it was
only on the last Griffmen's last
visit here that he said the Indians
pitching staff would fall apart
and that his team had a fine
chance to land in the first division.


Since his prophetic utteranceS
of July, the Griffmen have won
three out of four games played
with the Indians and the pitcher
who was lambasted today was one
who was blasted off the mound
in Washington last month.


Short Stay for GalehOuse


Cleveland pitted Dennis Gale
house, the young star who has
done his best work against the
Yankees this year but who never
has started against them, against
Whitehill, who was after his
twelfth victory of the season.


The Griffmen disposed of Gale
house in the first inning, making
six hits and five runs before Thor
ton Lee came in to stop the rata
tat-tat of base hits.


On August Is, in washington,
the Griffmen made nine runs off
GalehouSe in the first inning.
Yesterday they didn't do as well
but they made Steve ONeill OF
the Tribe sorry he took another
chance with his rookie.


Ben Chapman opened the game
with a double to right and scored
Immediately on a single to left by
Buddy Lewis. Then followed a
fusillade of hits that sent the In
dians staggering back on their
heels. Joe Kuhel scratched a
single off Galehouse'S glove, Stone
belted a clean single to center,
Cecil Travis doubled and Fred
Sington doubled before O'Neill
could rescue Galehouse.


Lee to Rescue


After Sington doubled, Lefty Lee
was substituted for GalehouSe and
he stopped the Griffmen dead
until the eighth when Whitehill
singled after Shanty Hogan had
doubled. Another run was added
| in the ninth on passes to Stone
and Sington and Miles single.
These runs were off Oral Hide
brand, the third pitcher the In
dams used in a futile effort to
stop the Washington attack.


While the Griffmen were bonn
harding the Cleveland hurlers, the
Indians were running up rapidly
mounting deficit against White
hill. The lefthander BANKED the
Tribe until the fourth when Earl
Averill drove the ball over the
right-field wall for his twenty-Sixth
home run of the campaign.


This hit helped Averill retain
his League batting laurels, the
Cleveland outfielder getting an
infield hit in the sixth and
drawing base on balls in the
eighth that led to the Red Skins
second tally. There were two
out when Averill walked. Lewis
booted Hal TroSky'S grounder
and Averill was able to complete
the circuit on Joe Vosmik's double
over Stones head.


Because it was ladies day at
League Park, 10000 eople

ing. The women cheered every
move the Indians made, appar-
emily failing to understand that
team that had been counted
out of the running in March was
standing favored pennant
threat on its already bashed-in
noggin.

Members of the North Randle
Community Citizens Association are
pleased with the portable schools
erected In their area to relieve over
crowding in the Benning School and
to save North Randle children the
long trip to the Benning School.


This Is the first year portables have
been tried. The children attending
the schools have made such salts
factory progress, however, that many
parents who continued to send their
children to the Benning School are
planning to enroll them In the port
ables in February.


While the general feeling Is that
portable schools do not take the place
of permanent grammar and junior
high schools, the citizens are for the
time satisfied.

-Jingling bells and one-horse

L. rather than the exception here
In Zakopane, Poland's popular Winter

An unknown wilderness village few
decades ago, Zakopane now has hotels.
a theater and automobiles and buses
for its streets, but travellers IN search
of a real experience still choose the
native sleighs for their outings. Carved
and gaily painted. these are the first
thing that strikes ones eye when one
arrives in Zakopane. The drivers are
Gorals, or mountaineerS, in white
trousers, deliberately embroidered, and
sheepskin waistcoats, with a little hat
perched jauntily on their heads, and
once their passenger is in they tuck
sheepskins around his legs, speak to
the horse and away the sleigh goes
gaily down the street.


The Zakopane region is also pleas
ant one in Summer, when boat trips
of three hours are made down the
Dunajec River to the frontier between
Czechoslovakia and Poland. The boats
used are about IA feet long and are
made of tree trunks, followed out and
bound together with fiber. AS for the
boatmen. they are the same noun
taineers in the same picturesque COS
TUNES that one sees in Winter, but
now they are intent on pointing out
the fine scenery and telling legends.


If the passengers are lucky, they
suddenly hear the sound of music and
see a peasant band appear around
river bend. Then singing children
wade out into the stream with a great
hoop Of flowers, under which the boat
passes, and Poland for moment be-

LEBANON, Ind. January 10-The
death knell of the coal oil lamp, the
stove-heated pressing iron, the Ian
tern and other antiquated farm utili-
ties has been rung in Boone County,
Ind.


With simple ceremony, the first pole
In one of the first rural electriflcation
projects in the United States was
erected yesterday on the west edge
of Lebanon. From it, and others
which will follow quickly, will be
strung the wires which will carry
electric current into some 1000 farm
homes.


Several hundred farmers, shivering
In ice and snow, watched Morris l..
Cooke, administrator of the Federal
Rural Electrification Administration,
turn the first shovelful of dirt.


Later, Cooke and Frederic I. Bar
rows of the Indiana State wide Rural
Electrification Membership Corp. told
the farmers, in the more comfortable
quarters of the high school, what they
may expect of the new projects.


Electrification of the farms under
the Federal plan-the Government ad-
vanced S567 1926 for the Boone County
project-will not interfere with the
operation of private business, the
speakers said. The project is intended,
It was explained, to give electricity to
farms which private utilities feel they
cannot profltably accommodate.


The Federal Government loaned the
money at per cent interest and will
allow 20 years for repayment.

A group Of workers besieged in the
wire mill of the strike-closed Wheel
ing Steel Corp. plant ate regular
meals today but did not know when
their food supply would be replenished
again.


Encountering no opposition, 16
sheriff's deputies went through the
picket lines late yesterday with food

crackers for SO hours.

nor company officials would say when
another attempt to send food in
would be made. Nor would they say
how much food they took in yester-
day or how many men were in the
wire mill.


Food shipments to some 200 guards
and workers inside the huge plant
stopped Tuesday when strikers and
guards battled around a train carry
ing supplies from the main plant to
the isolated wire mill. One guard
was killed.

of violepce continued today, when

NEW YORK. June 9-The Spring
potato crop rolled into this market
today ending for the time being the
likelihood Of "spud" famine. and
topping prices from the peaks for
several years established toward the
end of last week.


New-crop white potatoes, scores of
carloads of them, have been rushed
to the produce district for some half
dozen States in the last two days,
commission merchants reported.


Prices, which were above the SO
mark per barrel at the week end,
have dipped to around ST.


The scanty supplies, part of a Ma
tion-wide squeeze which has been de-
veloping for months. became partic-
ularly noticeable last Friday when
the Furness liner Fort Amherst, due
with 5000 bags from Nova Scotia,
went aground off the New England
Coast. Her cargo, the line said today,
had been salvaged with little damage.
The addition helped to ease the
pinched Eastern markets.

NEW YORK, December &c.
Through increased consumption due
to lower prices, the chemical industry
Is scoring record sales, and near
record earnings, according to q new
study appearing in Porr's Industry
and Investment Surveys.


One important factor is the trans
formation Of former waste materials
into valuable products. Buttressed
by sound capitalizations, adequate
liquid resources. low labor costs and
excellent research facilities, leading
manufacturers will continue to pros
per with extended industrial recovery.


Steady Rise Continues.


"As yet there Is no indication of q
slackening in the industry's rate Of
growth" the report continues. This
may be attributed to four underlying
factors:


"O Widely diversified markets for
products.


"(0 Conservative financial policies.


"(0 Installation Of production
economies.


go Practically unlimited possi-
bilities for new products and processes.


Competition forces continue keen,
but OF . less oppressive type than
those characterizing most other fields
of business. The industry's favorable
earnings record during the depression
also reflects the wisdom of policies
developed during the boom period.
Consequently, except in the fertilizer
and industrial alcohol fields. overex-
pansion with its attendant excessive
overhead costs and demoralizing trade
practices has not bedevilled the indus
try at any time since 1929.


Aggressive Research Cited.


Broadly speaking, the chemical in
dustry's profits depend upon sales vol
ume, and price trends have been gen.
orally downward, as operating econ.
omies are passed on to consumers.
However, the industry offers the out
standing example of successful ex-
pansion, due to aggressive research,
which has developed new products. new
processes and new uses for existing
products.


Even during the depression major
chemical organizations expanded
rather than curtailed their research
activities. As a result, they enjoy q
definite competitive advantage today.
In many instances, sales have sur
passed former peak levels despite the
fact that consuming industries are still
well below 1929 operating levels. Thus
chemical producers are in an ad-
mirable position to profit from con-
tinued recovery In general industry"

VALLADOLID. Spain, August 20
R.-Rebel army ranks were increased
tonight as reserves from dismissed
military classes responded to a recall
from the insurgent high command.


A total Of $4,000 reinforcements
was expected to be gained with the
influx Of reservists from the classes Of
1884 and 1885 called by Gen. Fran
cisco Franco and Gen. Emilio Mola.


The rebels already claimed two
thirds of the regular army of los 900
men under their command.


Even with this additional strength,
however. the insurgent forces, accord
ing to Gen. Mola's own estimate, will
be outnumbered by the government,
which he said has $4,000 men and
women under arms. Women are serv-
ing as cooks and nurses behind the
rebel lines, but none. he said. has
shouldered a rife.


Insurgent troops. as a general rule,
are far better equipped than the gov
ernment forces, partly because most
Of them were recruited from the reg
ular army and partly because the
rebels control the national arms man
ufacturing plant.

BY CONSTANTINE BROWN.
~ RESIDENT ROOSEVELT'S
- good neighbor policy with


Latin America, now placed
L above all else on the New Deal
international horizon, has recently
been going through an extremely deli
cate phase, which may affect our re-
lations on the American continent for
years to come.


1t is period of diplomatic and
economic jockeying between those two
powerful republics Of South America
Argentina and Brazil. The negotia-
tions between those two neighbors and
the United States are not unlike the
diplomatic dickering now In progress
between Great Britain. France and
Germany.


For years Brazil has been the tradi-
tional friend of the United States. No
matter how much Latin American
criticism was heaped on Washington
during the days of Nicaraguan inter-
vention and the oil notes to Mexico,
Brazil arose as our friend and cham
pion. Even at the Pan-American
Conference Of 1929 in Havana, when
Charles Evans Hughes fought battle
against terrific odds to prevent the
Pan-American nations from censoring
the United States on Intervention,
Brazil came forward with a stand
which blocked the resolution.


Then there is the Brazilian navy,
which for years has been trained by
American naval officers. When the
United States entered the World War,
Brazil automatically declared war also.
And when the United States declared
war on Spain, Brazil was the only
country to stand forth on continent
of Spanish nations and send two war
ships to the aid of the United States.


Unwritten Alliance Strained.


But within the last two years this
unwritten alliance has been strained
slightly by the new Roosevelt policy
of courting closer relations with
Argentina.


To appreciate properly what this
means, it is necessary to remember,
first, that Argentina and Brazil long
have been ardent and sometimes bitter
rivals: and. secondly, that Argentina
for years has been the chief critic
Of the United States in South America.


Argentina,s policy has been to ally
herself with Great Britain just as
faithfully AS Brazil allied herself with
the United States The motives in
each case were economic. The great
outlet for Argentine meat and, to a
lesser extent, wheat. is Great Britain.
just as the great outlet for Brazilian
coffee is the United States.


Moreover, British interests have
been almost inextricably woven into
the Argentine economic fabric. Most
of the railroads are British built and
owned; the banks are British, the
shipping lines, the brokerage houses,
the meat packing plants and even one
newspaper are British.


Into this essentially pro-British at
mosphere, Secretary of State Hull in
jected President Roosevelt's good
neighbor policy in the Autumn of
1888 with a special visit to President
Justo and Foreign Minister Saavedra
Lamas. Brazil Immediately became
suspicious. This suspicion changed
to mild resentment when Cordell Hull
rose on the floor of the Montevideo
Conference and followed the lead of
Saavedra Lamas in denouncing the
policy Of armed Intervention in the
affairs Of Latin American countries.


Brazil Left Holding the Bag.


Previously. the Brazilian delegate,
expecting the United States to take
its traditional stand for intervention,
had made a glowing speech regarding
its necessity, so that Mr.. Hull's re-
treat left him shamefacedly holding
the bag.


Since that time a series Of minor
incidents have popped up to mar the
old entente cordiale between the
United States and Brazil, two old ira
ditional friends of the Western Hem
sphere.

American naval advisers to Argentina.

Fascist big guns hammered Madrid's

day amid unconflrmed rumors that
insurgent Moors and Foreign Legion
naires had reached the Paseo de

These reports said the insurgents

defenders with heavy fire.

OUR bodies are equipped with tenn


perature organs. Some record only
cold temperatures. others only warm
temperatures. The so-called cold spots
are more numerous than the warm
spots. And these two sorts of organs
are as different as your eyes are from
your ears in the matter of recording
and interpreting experiences.


That cooling substance called men,
thol will excite the cold spots and pro-
duce no effect upon the warm spots.
So when you have headache, with its
accompanying fever you put some
menthol on your forehead. The cold
spots go into action and you feel bet
ter because you imagine that you are
getting rid of your fever. Even if you
are deceived about the actual state Of
affairs, the menthol has its virtue.
The general condition of feeling bet
ter" does react favorably upon your
nervous system and thus promotes re-
covery.


The old-fashioned mustard plaster
is another illusion. Mustard excites
only the warm spots, and so you
imagine that you are driving the cold
from your lungs by the application of
heat.


A temperature of 113 degrees Fab
renheit will stimulate both the warm
and cold spots. That's why you shiver
and get goose flesh in hot bath.

The Navy was in the market today
for 100000 pounds of copper. but
could find nobody willing to sell.


This strange situation was due,
Navy officials said, to the new Walsh
Healey Government contract act.


The act provides that concerns
which make contracts of more than
$4,000 with the Government must pay
prevailing" wages as determined by
the Secretary of Labor, must establish
q 40-hour maximum work week and
employ no child labor.


The Navy's bids were to be open ID
yesterday, but no bids appeared. Navy
officials Immediately made known they
would discuss the situation with Secre-
tary Of Labor Perkins.


Operating 48 Hours = Week.


Although no comment could be OBJ
tanned here directly from large copper
companies, persons usually well in
formed said many Western copper
mines were operating 48 hours week.


The Navy also disclosed that an un-
usually small number of bids were
submitted yesterday for the complete
East Coast fuel oil supply for the
Navy, War, Treasury. Commerce and
Labor Departments during the first
quarter of 1887.


Not more than two bids were sub
mitted for any one lot. No bid ap-
peared for one 17o,000-barrel order.


Only one bid was received for q
contract for $500 tons of steel to be
used in new ships under the Nays
building program. This bid, depart
ment officials said, was unsatisfactory.


Exemption Requests Received.


Although she had not been advised
off1cially of the copper, oil and steel
situations, Miss Perkins said both
Government purchasing agencies and
private businesses had made requests
for exemptions from the act.


The Navy Department, she said,
might ask for exemptions in the pres
ent cases.


Some Government officials said the
upswing in business the Nation over
might be more responsible than the
Walsh Healey act for an increasing
trend of private industry to steer clear
Of Government contracts.

KAMENZ, Germany, April AFTER
q day Of deep grief. 72-year-old Frau
Pauline Hauptmann said today: u
cannot understand it."


The mother of the convicted Lind
bergh baby killer sat throughout the
day in her little cottage with her
hands folded in her lap, her white
head bent.


It was the first time this week that
she had not toiled over her wash
board or with knitting needles to earn
her living.


Frau Hauptmann appeared stunned
all day long. ever since the time this
morning when friends told her Bruno
Richard had died in the electric chair
in New Jersey.


Neighbors put a friendly wall
around her. fearing she might collapse
under the strain.


They found that she neither an
swered nor reacted in any way to the
words spoken to her.


After she recovered from the first
shock she asked: did my son re-
ceive a final blessing?"


She lifted her head somewhat when
she was told he had walked to the
chair without confessing. Neighbors
said it buoyed her hope that he was
innocent.

The Prison Industries Reorganiza-
ton Board, one of the planning agen-
cies being financed by Federal funds,
soon will start an intensive survey OF
the industrial activity at District penal
and correctional institutions, District
officials announced today.


Request for the survey was made by
the Commissioners few days ago at
the suggestion of the Board of Public
Welfare. Welfare Director Elwood
Street advised the Commissioners the
Federal board already is engaged in
such surveys of institutions in 13
States.


The study will deal not only with
industrial operations and allied activi-
ties of the District penal institutions.
but also with the actual and potential
markets for the prison-made products.


James P. Davis, executive director
of the Federal agency, told the Com
missioners today the survey would be
completed by January /, If possible.
The Commissioners had asked that the
findings be available by that date so
they could consider them in connec-
ton with proposed appropriations for
the penal institutions for the next
fiscal year.


The Welfare Board told the Com
missioners it believed the survey would
result in development of more diver
sified and effective industrial plan and
improve the relations between the IN
dustrial activities and the training
of prisoners for occupations.


Street hopes the survey will give
the outline of q longtime. construc-
tive program for industrial operations.

Tourists who visit Banbridge this

THE Green Pastures" played in New

When it was time for the selection

It was at first announced that The

the Pulitzer prize, and after 73 weeks
in New York, it moved to Chicago,
where it played for nearly five months
more.


Then it toured the Middle West and

and continued success in every city.
Des Moines supplied the largest single
days business in the history of the
play, admissions amounting to 1000,

Tor performance of some $500.


The third year "The Green Pas

part of the Nation.


A second tour of the same area fol-

brought the production back to New

night, and the majority of New York

Warner Bros. finally bought "The
Green Pastures" for the screen, little
more than five years after that first
eventful showing in the Mansfield
Theater in New York.

many people will probably see the pic
ture, which will have its Washington
premiere Friday, August 7, at Warner
Bros Earle Theater. The theatrical

never-to-be-forgotten film spectacle.

NEW YORK, June 20-Commodity
prices bounded ahead this week with
drought headlines supplying most Of
the impetus.


The Associated Press weighted index
of IS important commodity prices ad-
vanced from 71.91 last week to 1901
and compares with TAI year ago.
This Is the sharpest rise experienced
by the index since the four month o
per cent decline began.


A recent Weather Bureau report
called attention to the fact that only
seven States had better than normal
rainfall during May-Texas, Kansas,
New Mexico. Louisiana, Florida, Ore
gon and Washington The parched
upper reaches of the Mississippi VAL
ley and southeast cotton States found
little call for umbrellas during the
period.


Crop deterioration in these areas is
important. but the extent is unknown.

fully in the rain last week. The At
lantic seaboard, much of the South
and large sections of the Midwest

showers. The Weather Bureau, how

Wheat in Critical Stage.

precarious moisture position, reached
a arifirol !, E,;o
responded to the threatened reduced
harvest by rocketing in all the impor-
tant markets. Bidding for supplies
at steadily higher prices, the trade
found quotations were more than per
cent higher at the close of the week.

Rye duplicated its spectacular rise,
was up about cents on the week.

mors that the Government had lqui-

to prod buyers into action.

decline that has carried them down
IS per cent in the last six months has,

accompanied in the betterment, while

THE Vienna Choir Boys sang their

audience which filled Constitution
Hall yesterday afternoon. Eighteen
of these youthful singers, directed by
Victor Gomboz. gave varieo program.
beginning with sacred music, through
q one act opera by Mozart, and clos
ing the program with group Of secu-
lar songs.


The young boys marched out with
folded arms, wearing vestments, and
after they grouped themselves. Mr..
Gomboz struck a chord and they sang
20! Say Can You See?" in English
distinct enough to be understood all
over the auditorium. 1t was such =
surprise that it took the audience some
seconds to realize it was the signal
to rise and stand at attention for the
national anthem.


The sacred numbers were all sung
without accompaniment and without
notes, in fact no printed music was
used by the singers, except for the
two solos of Franz Schubert, "Hark.
Hark, the Lark" and Hedge Roses.
which the singer announced IN ex-
cellent English, and for the piano ac-
compartment which Mr.. Gomboz
played for the operetta.

entire program with almost perfect
intonation, splendid tone and an evil
dent enjoyment to themselves, which
added much to the pleasure they gave
their hearers. Seldom Is such COM
plete and perfect poise seen In more
mature singers than these future citi-
zens of Austria displayed yesterday.

well balanced and the voices blend
beautifully, their singing OF the
sacred numbers following traditions
in their phrasing. shading and nnisn.

respective delegations to Chicago.

fled and later the local Republican
chieftain presented. a resolution
designating the committee headed

State committee for the District

referred to the executive COM
mittee for future action and the
action was taken last night.

of rock, rescuers reached an out
stretched hand, but could not extricate

timber to prevent another slide.

wick, his helper.


Bottrill was single, the other two
married.


Morden and Warwick were caught
with Bottrill when he made his regular
inspection shortly after midnight.
Nine men working nearby escaped.

text:
} SillieSt of the canards was the
hard-to-kill Eastern report that
Shirley Temple was a midget.


Even Hollywood fell for the
rumor that Bing Crosby, Gary
Cooper and Mae West were going
to withdraw from Paramount and
form a producing company Of
their own. The reported signing
of Jimmy Walker to head a film
organization received credence
here, too.


The most unfair rumors were
those concerning Loretta Young
and her illness.


And the story still crops up that
Ginger Rogers and Fred AStaire
are insanely jealous of each other
and will split as a team.


Hollywood has learned to shrug
and take it. Well, almost.

For the first time, the soldiers OF the
World War are in the key places at the
Republican National Convention. Four
years ago. they dominated the dele
gates seats; eight years ago. they were
lust coming in: twelve years ago, here
in Cleveland when Coolidge was NOM
mated, the World War veterans were
tip-toeing into the third line from
G. H. @.


Coolidge and Chairman Butler un-
doubtedly did the younger men good
turn at Cleveland in 1924. They dis
placed rather incontinently and with
out much punctility the old crowd with
the old quarrels that had dominated
the party for 20 years before. Coolidge
introduced the business man into the
control of the Republican party.


In that day. IL years ago, snappy,
we'll dressed young business men in
their middle 40s and early SOS crowded
out the f1shy-eyed, heavy -paunChed
saggy- -jowled Older statesmen who had
fought with Taft and Roosevelt in the
battle of Armageddon. Today these
hustling go-getters of the middle 20s
are now in their SOS and COS. They did
not stay long in politics, being busy
with the depression.


Like Eagle Scouts.


So the young World War soldier,
who came to learn the ropes dozen
years ago, is now running the ship.
Just lot .of starry-eyed Eagle
Scouts" said Sam Blythe, who has
seen every convention since the nomi-
nation of Harrison in 1892; as he
looked over the ponies scampering
around the track in the political hotels
today. This crowd" he said, looks
like covey of Raphaels cherubim,
all decked out in 81 seersucker pants
and collegiate coats covering their
wings


Like true Anglo-Saxon Colonists,
they are bringing their women with
them. Their women, good looking
young matrons who wear their
clothes we'll and prove what every
national crowd proves these days, that
there is no American millinery from





Main Street. They all dress alike. and
pretty niftily. too. They all have the
same kind of permanentS and the
same kind of shoes.


The more serious ones, who may be
easily spotted as delegates or national
committeewomen, glow a little more
gorgeouSly, blossom with somewhat
more effulgence and with here and
there just little more plumage than
would properly adorn pullets and with
little less dignity than setting hens
They live in twilight zone, these
professional women politicians and are
becoming more and more cult in the
political life of this continent.


Old Order Vanishes.


A generation ago, before women had
the ballot, their petticoats used to
show when they appeared at national
conventions. They were crusaders and
wore hats befltting noble causes-and
we're given to high shoes and high
ideals. They came advocating pro-
hibition, equal suffrage, minimum
wage laws, and the abolition of child
labor. They relied more on statistics
than sex appeal to win their way.
That crowd and those days have van
ished.


The pre-convention crowd in Cleve-
land today is cross-section of Amer
lean life. There is no difference be-
ween the urban, suburban and rural
types of woman-and small difference
among the men. Sartorial mass pro-
duction has broken down class and
geographic differences.


So much for the exterior. The spirit
of the crowd that is gathering for the
Republican National Convention is
rather more serious than usual and
absolutely without factional alignment
One hears no wrangles in the lobbies
OF the hotel. One sees no evidence Of
bitterness in the bed rooms where the
men sit and smoke and swap glittering
lies about the availability and in
Vulnerability of their candidates.
Among the delegates-and possibly q
third Of them are here-the third
which takes leadership-there is no
Wrangling, no recrimination and
precious little whispering and scandal
izing. Caucuses meet and wrangle all
night and jower about trivial matters.
but nothing is accomplished, no one
cares.


Few Political Gimcracks.


The bands will come tomorrow and
the stunts of the various candidates
will trot through the streets and hotel
lobbies. But they will be meager-
few bands, few political gimcracks
The truth is, no one has any money
In this campaign. Indeed, less money
has been spent by the candidates than
ever was spent in national campaign
before. If the tell-tale evidences of
political penury in the big hotels are
to be trusted. The great banners, the
monster flags that should be flappine
across the Cleveland streets, are miss
ing. Printed matter, cards, handbills.
curious little gadgetS that pass from
hand to hand in ordinary conventions.
celebrating various gags and wise
cracks. have not appeared.


The crowd is serious, without being
Solemn. One hears more talk about
platform planks than about candi-
oates. Possibly this dearth of talk
about candidates is due tn the obv,o,,.

7426 on Thursday from 1886 last

This turn-about in the recent down

ginning Of the disastrous drought two
years ago. On this basis some doubts

were covered last week.

more than point for the first time
this year. Lack of rain in the grain

rye. oats and cotton.

higher levels. including butter lard.
cocoa and eggs. The latter responded
to reports that takings last month il

Chicago jumped more than Sc per

ment.


With cattle, hog and lamb prices
pushing ahead, the live stock index
scored the largest increase, with one
exception, for the year to date.

EDMONTON, Alberta, November
19.--The Alberta government ordered
a minimum wage law for men into
effect yesterday and announced five
industrial codes.


The codes related to the wholesale
business, the automotive trade, Ed
monton district bakers, BARRIERS and
photo finishers.


Under the minimum wage law, a
board of three will be appointed to in
quire into industries, set wage
schedules and enforce regulations.
Enabling legislation last April pro-
vided for the codes.


The wage law applies to all in
dustries except farm, labor and
domestic servants. Alberta has had a
minimum wage law for women for
sometime.


The wholesale code announced its
objective was to prevent, except under
justiflable circumstances, selling from
wholesaler to a consumer. An
advisory board from the industry
itself will be appointed to assist in
enforcing the regulations.

mand claimed control today of vast

Graziani's mechanical column 275

tier, continues with the motorized

SALEM, Oreg., August 1.-Shattered
windows piles of knives and clubs and
cluttered prison yard gave evidence
today Of riot in which 700 convicts
unsuccessfully broke for freedom from
the Oregon State Penitentiary.


One prisoner was killed and two
were wounded as guards fred to quell
the mob, maddened by word that the
Circuit Court had upheld an attorney
generals opinion barring releases from
prison at the expiration of minimum
sentences except after formal action
Of the Parole Board and Governor.


Word of the ruling reached the
convicts yesterday. Two of them went
to the commissary and ordered the
cooks to stop work. Several score
others began piling food in the yard
where 600 more were spending rest
period. Leaders began yelling and
the cry gained volume.


Frank Tilson, serving q f1ve-year
term for burglary and assault on an
officer, shouted: Come on, guys
let's make q break for it,


A sharp command to halt was ig-
nored.


One guard fired into the air as the
frenled crowd moved toward the
walls. Then some of the prisoners
passed the deadline 80 feet inside the
barricade.


Guard H. H. Corey fired into the
crowd. Three men slumped. AS the
prisoners apparently were preparing
for another rush State policemen ap-
peared on the walls with tear-gas
bombs.


The convicts quieted and a moment
later marched back to their cells.
Then bedlam broke loose. Prisoners
shouted, threw clubs and knives
through windows and between the
bars. The weapons were taken from
the butcher shop and commissary.


Thomas Baughn, so, murderer, died
an hour after the riot. James Ham
ilton, SO. another killer, was shot
through the lung. Joseph Dupray,
"a, burglar, was shot in the hand.

COLUMBUS, Ohio. January %
Labor interests and legal authorities
Of several States watched closely to-
day as Ohio completed its briefs in
case which will determine whether
the United States may delegate to
States permission to enact prohibitory
laws involving interstate commerce.


Attorney General John w. Bricker
will lead fight in the United States
Supreme Court next week against the
appeal Of Asa H. Whitfield of Ala
bama from a conviction for violating
State law prohibiting sale of prison.
made goods In open markets


Case Called Novel.


Bricker described the case, a test
of the State law and the Federal
Hawes- Cooper act. as lone of the most
novel in recent legal history and one
of great importance to labor interests
everywhere"


The Cooper law, enacted by
Congress in 1929, gave the States the
right to impose the same restrictions
against prison made goods coming
into their open markets as the States
themselves imposed upon goods manu-
factured in their own prisons.


Ohio passed prohibitory law in
compliance with the Federal act.
Whitfield, an agent of the State Of
Alabama. was fined $25 in Cleveland
Municipal Court for violating that law
October 2. 1894.


Violations Charged.


Whitfield pleaded, when arraigned,
that the Ohio law not only violated
the State constitution, but also pro-
visions of the United States Constitu-
ton guaranteeing equal rights and
protection to all States and citizens
and giving Congress the sole power to
regulate interstate commerce.


He contended Congress could not
delegate its authority to the States
to regulate interstate commerce


The Ohio Supreme Court dismissed
his appeals


Both New York and Minnesota,
which have laws similar to the Ohio
statute. have joined Ohio in attempt
ing to uphold the Federal Hawes-
Cooper act and their own State laws.

The interhigh school football
series for 1885 is an event of his
tory now, but to the countless
thousands who were in on the

les; Charlie Jones, guard; Sam

times for Western; Kidweu for his

ern team that reached its heights

ton for his rise as Central'S most
potent ground gamer and threat

centers. Bill Kemp and Frank
Hodge were leaders. Kemp is Sc
lected for his fighting play

incidentally, is the first Eastern
center to be picked since the days

FORT PLAIN. N. Y, July "A
tour of the Northeastern United
States is complete, townspeople here
boast, only when it includes the Mo-
hawk Valley 1t is one of New York's
most historic and picturesque regions
and those who know it through many
visits come year after year to the
land haunted by the shades of the
mighty Mohawks. Sir William john
son, Gen. "Honikol' Herkimer and
the men who went to their death with
him in the dramatic Revolutionary
American victory in the forest of
Oriskany.


The new mingles with the old, the
mighty pathways of commerce are
lined with ancient houses and the
sites of the thrilling and tragic his
torical episodes which make the Mo-
hawk Valley romantic region.


Baronial Halls.


The Gen. Herkimer home at Little
Falls, Guy Park at Amsterdam and
johnson Hall at Youngstown and Fort
johnson both the only baronial halls
in America, are interesting Colonial
brick, frame and stone houses, with
important historical collections open
free to the public. Fort Johnson's
museum holds a Mohawk dugout and
also the finest Mohawk Indian col
lectionS in existence. Here, also are
relics which seemingly bring to life
the ancient Holland Dutch life of
the Eastern HohaWk Valley.


The lure of great. rugged forest
crowned hills combine with the charm
of the pastoral scenes.


The Little Falls gorge, the Moses" 4"
rising in beetnng cliffs high above
the fertile fatlands, the Mohawk's
teeming river commerce, above rail-
ways and highways, and the great
'hogsback" of Fall Hill, rising 1000
feet above the river on the backbone
of the Appalachian range, are typi-
cal features of the Mohawk Valleys
constantly varying landscape.


Vast Recreation Areas.


The foothills of the Adirondacks
break from the upper northern slopes
of the Mohawk, while to the south
the Cherry Valley hills loom in solid
phalanx as the northern outposts of
the Catskills Main roads lead from
the valley to both of these vast recrea-
tional areas.


One of Americas greatest trans
portation belts traverses the Mohawk
Valley from east to west-railroads,
highways. barge canal and the Buff
falo-Cleveland airmail and the
American Airlines transcontinental
airway.


The 70 towns which line the 100
miles Of river, between Schenectady
and Rome, house some of Americas
greatest industries Schenectady
Amsterdam, Johnstown, Gloversville.
Little Falls. Utica and Rome are
Mohawk Valley cities, whose manu-
factured products have Nationwide
renown.

MANNHEIM, Germany (R.-White
music notes printed on a black back
ground have replaced the traditional
black notes on white in the orchestra
pit Of the local civic theater and opera
house.


An engineer charged with improv-
ing the lighting for the orchestra found
that the reflection of the music stand
lights on the white pages often pro-
voked quarrels between conductor and
stage manager. The stage manager
objected to the interference of Or
chestra pit lights with his efforts at
darkening the stage The conductor
insisted his musicians could not play
in the dark.


By printing the notes in white on
q non-glossy black paper, all quarrels
were stopped. The Mannheim or.
chestra pit is almost dark. Lights fall
upon the diminutive white notes only.


The musicians say the white notes
are restful to the eye. The stage man.
ager can conjure up balmy nights for
stage sweethearts without having the
illusion destroyed by reflected lights
from the pit.

ATHENS, May 23.-The little
known Greek islands that are scat
tered along the mainland often are
overlooked by tourists, yet each holds
a diversity of interest. There Is San
torin, island of fire and wine. There
Is Crate, with its heavily wooded
mountains and vast. reconstructed
palace and ruins. Lying close to Asia
Minor there is Chios of the mastic
groves, those peculiar little trees that
drop glittering white gum, and Samos,
noted for its wines.


Mytilene, where Sappho lived, and
closer to the mainland lies Skyros,
where quaint furniture is hand-carved
and bright embroideries are made


Spetsae, where fashionable Atheni-
ans go for the Summer, is an ideal
place from April to November. The
shepherds pipe to their straying fiocks,
the fishing boats set out at twilight,
their orange and white sails Tapping
to the breeze. The hotel Is splendid
and there are numberless rocky coves
and beaches in which to bathe; there
is tennis and sailing and, in season,
dinner and dancing under the pines,
beside the cool and crystal waters.

and fight their way into Madrid.


Insurgent artillery, operating in the
vicinity of the Toledo and Segovia
bridges, fired scattered houses in the
extreme southwestern part of the
capital.


A large part of the district already
was evacuated.


The Moors and Legionnaires were
ordered to ford the river to the south
of the Toledo bridge because the
spans were reported to have been
mined.


Reinforced Fascist troops assaulted
the northwestern sector of the city,
but the extent of their penetration was
not known to correspondents.


Just before dawn, during a short
pause in the almost incessant battle,
thousands Of Fascist and Carlist re-
serves filed into the front lines of the
insurgent army.


Oflcers expected the onslaught
would drive stubbornly resisting gov
ernment militiamen from the city-side
approaches of the mined Manzanares
River bridges back into the capitals
own streets.


Artillery shells dropped into the
government entertainments at closely
spaced intervals, while the Fascist
front lines peppered the defense forces
with machinegun and rifle fire.


The attack, insurgent commanders
said, was the prelude to one of the
biggest battles of the civil war.


Fascist artillery showered shells
into the Madrid first-line trenches to
support infantry charges which ad-
vanced the attackers positions to the
banks of the river on the south side
of the city.


whitening fire blasted a hole in

reported to have almost wiped out
a Socialist battalion of women.


Heavy casualties were inflicted the
whole length OF the government line

JUNEAU, Alaska, Nov. %.
IN.s.).-Dozens of persons
were believed buried alive in
the wreckage of three apart
ment houses and other build
ings today when an avalanche
roared down from Mt. Roberts,
burying Front Street, Juneau S
main thoroughfare, under 10
feet of rock and other debris.


Hundreds Of citizens, awak-
ened by the catastrophe, were
digging frantically in the mud
and rock for the victims, includ-
ing many children, who were
given little chance Of survival.


Five bodies were removed from
the wreckage of several buildings:
rescue workers reported.


Engineers of the Alaska highway
commission and the great Alaska
Juneau Gold Mine rushed power
digging equipment into submerged
Front Street today.


Under supervision of police, fire
men and Coast Guard officers,
work proceeded with caution, to
avoid possible further injury to
living persons entombed in the
mass.


Ten Found Injured


Ten persons injured in the
avalanche were taken to the small
Juneau hospital.


All were removed from the edge
of the Shiny mass. Little hopes
were held for others believed
buried farther back.


Digging the debris away was
slow as more mud slid down the
mountain side.


Not before tonight, police esti-
mated, will it be known how many
persons died in the catastrophe.
Some, it was believed, might have
fled from the buildings, only to be
overwhelmed by the mud and
rocks which hurtled down upon
them.


Town Cut Off

A solemn, Sorrowful tribute was
paid to the late Speaker Joseph
w. Byrns today, with President
Roosevelt and other dignitaries,
including foreign diplomats. join
ing in reverent state funeral serv.
ices in the House chamber.


Mr.. Roosevelt bowed his head
as prayer was uttered for the
late House leader and stared
fixedly as speakers eXtoIled his
memory.


Throughout the brief but dig
nified services high officials and
members of Congress evidenced
their grief for the passing of the
genial, gaunt Tennesseean who
rose to hold the third highest
office in the nation.


Respected by All


The services reflected the respect
which all official Washington,
without regard to party or affilia-
lions, bore for the late Speaker,
whose death from a cerebral hem.
orrhage early yesterday shocked
the Capital.


The career of "Joe" Byrns, who
began life as farm boy but whose
good fellowship, keen mind and
interchangeable energy attracted all.
brought him rich reward from
appreciative fellow TennesseeanS
and colleagues in Congress


With Mr. Roosevelt, who planned
to accompany Speaker Byrns'
body to Nashville late today for
burial rites tomorrow, were Secre-
taries Stephen Early and Marvin
Mcintyre and his aides, Col. Edwin
| M. Watson and Capt. Paul Bastedo.
Flowers Cover Coffin


The body Of the late Speaker
lay in a huge, bronze coffin in
front of the Speakers rostrum.
from which he ruled the House
with a mixture of kindness ana
firmneSs.


Great banks of flowers, green
plants and palms almost covered
it. They came from colleagues.
from officials and from diplomats.
A touching tribute was paid by
the House page boys, who knew
the Speaker as Uncle joe" Their
nickels and dimes purchased a
large spray of roses.


Just before the services, more
than 400 members of the House
and Senate filed silently past the
bier.

suspended, and several bus lines

Washington county in it's grip.


While hundreds Of men are busy
digging this city out from under
11-inch snow, IA State highway
plowS operating, all day yesterday
and last night, have been able to
keep open the national highway
between this city and Washington.


Telegraph lines and poles were
reported down and a number of
county roads are reported drifted
shut this morning. Route II be-
tween Hagerstown and Winchester
is reported drifted shut in several
! places.

DORCHESTER, New Brunswick,
September 23.-Two brothers-Arthur
Bannister, 19. and Daniel, 20-were
hanged together today for killing q
woodsman-squatter during the kid
naping of his infant daughter for
extortion plot.


Resigned to death after rejec-
ton Of the appeals for clemency, the
brothers walked silently to the gal
lows. where they stood back to back
rs the nooses were placed over their
heads.


Its too tight, I can't pray" COM
planned Daniel shortly before the
traps were sprung simultaneously at
2:06 am. Atlantic daylight time
(l2:o6 am Eastern standard time).


Given Single Coffin.


Both were pronounced dead at 2:27
am. Their bodies we're cut down and
placed together in a single pine coffin
covered with black cloth. The same
ropes used for the execution lowered
the coffin into grave in the prison
yard, so yards from their cell.


Their final visitors before the death
walk began were their father and two
sisters.


Il won't see you any more, but be
good girls" Arthur told his sisters.


The brothers were convicted of
killing Phillip Lake, 30-year-old
woodsman living near Pacific juno
ton, New Brunswick. The crown
charged the Bannister brothers were
responsible for Lakes death during
the abduction of his four -months-old
daughter last January.


Mrs. May Bannister, their mother,
wanted the baby to aid in an alleged
extortion plot against two men who,
the crown charged, were under moral
obligation to her.


Kidnap Plan Devised.


The prosecution during the BROTH
ers' trial asserted Mrs. Bannister at
tempted to fake motherhood by ap-
pearing with life-size baby doll. Her
effort to get money from the two
men with the doll failed. 1t was
charged, and she, her two boys, and
her 15-year-old daughter, Frances,
devised the plan to kidnap the Lake
baby.


During the kidnapping, Lake was
killed. his common-law wife fatally
injured and his young son left to die
outside their lonely cabin in Mid
winter, the prosecution alleged.


The brothers were charged with
killing only Lake and were found
guilty in separate trials. Mrs. Ban
mister was convicted of harboring the
stolen child and was sentenced to
serve three and one-half years in the
penitentiary. Frances Bannister has
been charged with abducting the Lake
baby and her trial set for Friday.

Maryland" As the body left the

grave.

Diocese of Maryland, conducted the
services.

timore's city hall tolled. Flags were
-masted over the entire State, and
State and local Offices were closed.

Greenmount Cemetery where burial

grave while brief prayers were being
said, one woman was stricken fatally

Monday morning in his apartment

BEIRUT. Syria. June 27.-Young
Syrian Arabs added their support to-
day to the Nationalist campaign
against British and Jews in Palestine


The Syrian leaders urged Arab kings
10 support actively their brothers in
the Holy Land and strengthened a
commercial boycott already organized
In their country.


Many merchants cut of shipments
of goods to Palestine Jews and young
native vigilantes erected blockade
against truckloads Of produce.


The widespread sympathy move
nent. designed to aid Palestine Arabs
to win satisfaction from the British
administration against Jewish immi-
grafton and land ownership, has had a
serious effect on Beirut trade,


Land Transportation Checked.


Land transportation was becoming
virtually impossible between Palestine
and Beirut, officials said.


Financial sources asserted many
merchants in the Holy Land have
stopped buying goods in Syria since
the outbreak nearly three months ago
of the Arab general strike in Palestine.
. Obligations which Palestine dealers
contracted remained unpaid and
Syrian merchants, in some instances,
have sought loans to pay their own
bills.


To complcate the situation, the
Syrians have their own movement
against French rule under a League
Of Nations mandate. problem which
the French government in Paris now
has under consideration.

French military forces in Syria
have been heavily reinforced lately,
bringing their estimated strength to
